subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REPORT ON DISMISSAL OF MESSRS. CHO, CHEW AND McGUIRE BY CN TELECOMMUNICATIONS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provision of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Within one year, three men, Messrs. Cho, Chew and McGuire, employed by CN Telecommunications have been dismissed and their dismissal is in obvious violation of the company and union agreement which states that an employee cannot be discharged until his case has been thoroughly reviewed and he has been advised of the reasons for such a review. Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley (Mr. Nowlan):
That this House instruct the Prime Minister to ask the Solicitor General for a full report on the involvement of the RCMP in this matter, request that the Minister of Labour investigate the firing of these men in relation to Section five (5) of the Canada Labour Code, and also that he order the Ministers of Transport and Communications to ascertain what input their respective departments had in these dismissals.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister. Considering that the most recently published Gallup poll indicated that 71 per cent of Canadians believe that there is now sufficient U.S. capital in Canada and 58 per cent of our population want the government to take steps to buy back majority control of major U.S. firms, can the Prime Minister say why the government, in bringing in its regulations to implement the Foreign Investment Review Act, brought in regulations which, to paraphrase what the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce said on Friday, will not change in all likelihood in absolute terms the amount of U.S. investment in the Canadian economy, and further, why specific measures were not announced by the government to move in the direction in which Canadians clearly want the government to move?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Postmaster General. In view of the fact that bargaining between the Post Office and the Canadian Union of Postal Workers is at the conciliation board stage, which is an extremely important stage for discovery of a basis for a peaceful and mutually satisfactory settlement, and in view of the government's often repeated hope that collective bargaining can take place between the employer and employee without resort to strike or lockout, and in view of the minister's well-publicized tirade against the democratically elected leadership of CUPW in calling them dishonest, deceptive and irresponsible, will the minister explain to this House why he has deliberately prejudiced the very sensitive and important deliberatings of the conciliation board by engaging in yet another round of counter-productive and frankly childish name-calling?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
subtopic: REQUEST FOR EXPLANATION OF MINISTER'S ATTITUDE TOWARDS UNION LEADERS-SUGGESTED REMOVAL OF MINISTER FROM OFFICE
speechtext: The hon. gentleman should know that no conciliation board has been set up yet. Second, I will admit my words may have sounded harsh. But I owe the hon. member an explanation. Some weeks ago in the House of Commons I was charged by the union with not providing adequate personnel in the department for processing grievances. I rectified that situation, and the grievances concerning the Montreal workers who were suspended have been on the desk of the deputy minister for over three weeks in the hope and anticipation that in case any of these suspensions were too severe, a review would reduce them to a minimum. The unions in question, despite the invitation of my department, have on three occasions postponed these negotiations and have now notified us that they will be unable to appear to plead for these workers until some time in August.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is true that there is a shortage of dentists in the Northwest Territories. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, earlier the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro) asked me about my visit to the Secretary General at the United Nations on Friday. I confirm that the visit did take place and my main purpose in seeing the Secretary General was to discuss the UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders. In the course of that discussion I advised the Secretary General of the United Nations that Canada does not wish to proceed with the Fifth UN Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders this year.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext: I have sought the Secretary General's co-operation in obtaining a postponement of the congress, and he has undertaken to study the situation in order to clarify the position. In the government's view, this congress cannot be held successfully anywhere this year.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext:
Hon. members will recall that at the fourth congress held in Kyoto in 1970, the Government of Canada, in consultation with the province of Ontario, proposed that the venue of the next congress be Toronto, in September of 1975. This proposal was accepted by delegations and subsequently confirmed by the General Assembly. Since that time, however, there has been a steady deterioration of the atmosphere in which international conferences are held. I need hardly mention the discord which marred the sixth special session and the last regular session of the General Assembly, the recent conferences of the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, UNIDO, and of the International Labour Organization, ILO, as well as the International Women's Year conference in Mexico a few weeks ago.
Whereas a minimum of co-operation is essential to any progress in the international field, we have witnessed lately excessive confrontation on issues that were not related to the subject matter of conferences. The ingredi-
Crime Conference
ents are well known: racialism in Southern Africa, the Middle East conflict, producer-consumer relations and the full range of economic development problems subsumed under calls for a "New World Economic Order". Canada believes that these are very real and difficult problems which must be dealt with urgently, in the appropriate international institutions, before they poison the body politic of the United Nations family; and let there be no doubt that we consider it necessary and desirable that political factors take their proper place even in the most technical of conferences. But they must meet some test of relevance, and in recent United Nations conferences this has clearly not been the case.
Hon. members are well aware that in respect of the Toronto congress on crime prevention, which was to take place next September, one of these issues had already become paramount. It arose from the resolution adopted in November, 1974, by the General Assembly, with Canada dissenting, inviting the Palestinian Liberation Organization, PLO, to attend its sessions as a permanent observer and, in a similar capacity, conferences convened under the auspices of the General Assembly or other organs of the United Nations. Accordingly, the Government of Canada was informed by the United Nations secretariat some time ago that observers from the PLO had been invited to attend the fifth congress on crime prevention and that the Canadian authorities were expected to allow entry, sojourn and exit to these participants.
Needless to say, it is with reluctance that the government has decided to seek postponement of the congress, but we concluded that it would not be possible, in present circumstances, to hold a successful congress on crime prevention in Canada or anywhere else. We are all aware of the public outcry for or against the admission to Canada, for this congress, of observers from the Palestinian Liberation Organization. We have all been worried by its divisive effect upon Canadian public opinion. We could not ignore the risk of public disorders. These factors would have led any government to reconsider a decision to host an international conference. But in the final analysis, two factors dominated in our discussions. The first was the inevitable intrusion of unrelated political considerations into the proceedings of the congress. The second was the re-escalation of violence in the Middle East and the consequent spread of its bitterness into Canada and subsequently into the congress itself.
It is obvious that such intrusion of the Middle East conflict, by adding to the already hopeless confusion between civil crimes and acts of war, would distort and subvert the purposes of what has essentially been up to now, and should remain, a technical meeting of experts from all countries, striving to develop international cooperation in a field of vital importance to the rule of law and to public order everywhere. As host country, we felt that Canada had assumed a major responsibility for the success of this congress, and in such an unfavourable political climate we did not see how we would possibly carry out our responsibility. I should add that we were also concerned about the coincidence of the congress with the seventh special session of the General Assembly on development and international economic co-operation, since the contentious atmosphere of one would in all likelihood seep into the other.

July 21, 1975

However, after an extensive review of the government's domestic and international obligations, we decided to inform the Secretary General of the United Nations that we did not want to be relieved of the responsibility for holding this congress but, rather, wished to postpone it. We did not want to withdraw our invitation to the United Nations, and we tried to avoid any steps which might have called into question our long-standing commitment to the principles of the United Nations. I emphasize that Canada's willingness to participate in and contribute to the operations of United Nations agencies remains undiminished.
The respite obtained by postponement must be effectively used by all to bring about sufficient improvement in attendant political conditions so that we may have reasonable assurances that technical conferences such as the fifth United Nations congress on crime prevention will be useful and productive. We hope that current negotiations for the reduction of tensions between some of the parties to the Middle East conflict will prove successful in coming months, and we will actively support the continuing efforts of the parties directly involved and of the United States government toward that goal.
Furthermore, the next General Assembly of the United Nations will provide an opportunity to affirm the principle of universality as a fulfilment of what ought to be a basic aim of the United Nations. More specifically, we will resist any attempt to exclude Israel or any other country from the proceedings of the General Assembly.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext:
Acceptance of this principle would guarantee the status of Israel within the community of nations and thus remove one cause of instability in the area. So that in requesting the postponement of the congress, Canada is not shirking its responsibilities but actually taking on new ones. Through new initiatives, both bilateral and multilateral, the government will try to improve the political situation in the Middle East and in the United Nations, notably through our participation in the next session of the General Assembly which may be crucial for the future of the organization, given the fundamental character of the issues on which debates are expected to focus. Canada will consult with other interested countries on the ground rules governing technical discussions in United Nations arenas. Either independently or in co-operation with others, we will attempt to formulate and seek support for an effective resolution in the General Assembly on this question.
I also intend to accept, during the autumn, outstanding invitations to visit a number of countries in the Middle East. These visits, which the government already considered most useful for strengthening our relations with this region of the world, have taken a new urgency following the difficulties we encountered in holding the U.N. congress on crime prevention. The House can be assured that I will take this opportunity to solicit the views of my hosts on these difficulties and seek their views on the United Nations as a universal forum and an effective international instrument.

Hon. members should note that our decision to seek the postponement of the congress for the reasons stated is consistent with the policy of the government on the Middle East. We will continue to cultivate, as we have done in the past, friendly and co-operative relations with all states in the region and to attach great importance to the development of these relations. Likewise, Canada has tried in the past to maintain a balanced and objective approach to the Middle East conflict and will continue to do so. We have always supported and defended the right of the state of Israel to exist in peace with its neighbours, behind secure and recognized borders. We have stated our conviction that no peaceful and stable solution to this regional conflict can be found without the participation of the Palestinians and the just settlement of their claims.
We have condemned the use of violence as a political instrument or as a means of retribution. We have partic-pated in all UN peacekeeping and cease-fire supervision missions in the Middle East and contributed to the United Nations relief operations for Palestinian refugees. We have advocated, and continue to advocate, the full implementation of Security Council resolution 242. All of this, therefore, continues to be government policy.
We are confident that the initiatives to be taken by Canada and other countries on the future of the United Nations and the Middle East will lead to a different atmosphere in which the postponed Fifth United Nations Congress on the Prevention of Crime and the Treatment of Offenders can be held in Canada, at a time to be decided upon, with sufficient assurances of success. It was agreed with the Secretary General of the United Nations that we should consult further on this question, and I expect to be in touch with him later this week.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME

Mr. Speaker, having heard the lengthy statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), I can only conclude that the minister is becoming more and more adroit in the art of diplomacy, of course with a little help from the opposition. It is obvious that we are here in the presence of what could be called dynamic leadership. Issues are not settled, they are postponed, and they are postponed in such a way as to imply, for instance, that in the future no technical meetings of the United Nations will be able to take place unless this issue has been resolved.
I find it strange to hear the minister say to the House that he does not know if the conference will not be held. He has only approached the Secretary General, and the minister said: "He has undertaken to study the situation in order to clarify his position." That is all we know. What will the Secretary General say? What will be his decision? Nobody knows. How long will this conference be postponed? Nobody knows. Will it take place in six months' time, or a year? Will it take place elsewhere? In another sentence the minister said: "It cannot be a successful congress on crime prevention, in Canada or anywhere else." Must we draw the conclusion that the government is now taking the position that for months and months ahead, unless the Middle East conflict is resolved, there
July 21, 1975

can be no meaningful conferences of the United Nations, whether on crime prevention or anything else, within Canada or elsewhere in the world? That is a question to which we would like to receive an answer.
We are pleased to know that where Mr. Kissinger has failed, the minister would probably succeed.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME

speechtext:
-by helicopter or otherwise, we certainly wish him good luck. However, in the meantime I find it very strange that the government has come to this decision, not because it is good for the country that this conference should not take place at this time, but because we all know what friction has already been caused. We all know that this decision will be viewed by many Canadians as a postponement, but at least also a guarantee that there will be security for our citizens and there will be no violence in September in Toronto. That is one thing which is sure. On the other hand, this decision should not be viewed by Canadians of Arab descent, for instance, as a slight or any expression of a partisan position. Rather, it should be viewed as an expression by the people of Canada of our concern for the continued rule of law and the continued commitment to a peaceful society in which all Canadians enjoy the freedom to express their own views.
Therefore, on this basis, because the government has been attentive to what has been said by the opposition, by leaders in government, by the provincial government of Ontario, by police chiefs, by the bar association and by the people of Canada, and has reached the decision that for the moment no conference should be held, we are grateful. However, when will the issue be resolved, and in what manner? What will be the impact of that government decision on the future of our participation in the United Nations? For the moment we expect more answers. I doubt whether we will receive them, but we expect something different from the government in the form of leadership and something more substantive than simply hoping that the problem will disappear with time.

. . . in due course. And considering the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it may be a good thing that the government take a lesson from this situation. The government waited too long. I do hope, Mr. Speaker, that the government will learn from this problem by paying greater attention to the claims made by the opposition as well as to suggestions it may submit to the House and that, secondly it will try a more dynamic type of leadership than our present one, which smacks of procrastination.

I should like to call the attention of the House to this. We said that the PLO, unfortunately, continues at the present time to include in its covenant or constitution a statement of its basic aims, which includes the liberation of the whole of Palestine as it existed before the surrender of the mandate by Britain, to be secured by a relentless, armed struggle with no compromise. This, I think, constitutes a fundamental commitment to destroy the state of Israel.
In addition to that, it is a fact, whether people like it or not, that the PLO has relied in the past upon terrorist actions directed at innocent people many of whom had no connection whatsoever with Palestine or Israel. We say, if the PLO is willing to indicate that the destruction of Israel, a sovereign independent state recognized by the United Nations, is no longer its objective, and to state it will proceed to seek its aims of an independent Palestine through negotiations, and forgo terrorism, then the situation would change fundamentally and a new approach would be taken.
The government, in these circumstances, has called for the postponement of the United Nations congress on the prevention of crime. Normally we would not applaud the government for postponing it. It is a technique that is too frequently used by this government, and others as well, to push problems under the rug, but in this particular case we believe the decision for postponement was a wise one. We think that to carry on with this congress under the present circumstances in Canada would have done no good to the cause of any of the parties to it, or any of the United

Nations, or of world peace. We think we are wise to say "not under these circumstances", but if a new situation develops, say a year from now, we would take a different attitude to the matter.
I note the reference in the statement by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen)-and this is what we are relying on-that the interim period is to be used for a real effort to solve some of the problems that have existed. There has been too much pushing aside of the problems. We do not delude ourselves that there are any easy solutions, but we do say this year must not be allowed to pass without continued efforts to mobilize world opinion to see if difficulties can be solved by negotiation. With the prospect of war in the Middle East and the possible escalation into world war, there are few other greater threats, to my knowledge, than the present situation in the Middle East. Now we hope we are going to have a breathing spell in which to deal with the matter.
I just want to add that in what we say we are in no way undermining the United Nations. The views of the majority of the General Assembly are, of course, entitled to great respect, but in my view the basic principles of the charter are even more important. They call for the respect and integrity of member nations. Until those who participate in international conferences are willing to accept that principle, international conferences cannot hope to succeed. In our view the United Nations is essential, but we think it is human to err and the UN can, and does, err. We think the time has come for people of good will around the world, and in Canada in particular, to rally behind the UN and show in every way that we propose to support it.
Mr. Speaker, this statement is not clear on what the government would do if the postponement cannot be arranged with the authorities in the United Nations. We in this party want to make it clear that whether the UN agrees or not, this conference should be postponed until the conditions we have suggested, the abandonment of terrorism and the willingness of the PLO to give up its objective of the destruction of the state of Israel, are clearly stated. If this is done, a new situation will arise and a new day of peace may dawn.

Mr. Speaker, I regret not receiving a copy of the minister's statement before three o'clock. Indeed, I did not receive it at all, so that I was unable to examine it.
I understand, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian government was in a way yielding to some pressures coming from a source or another, but especially from one. Postponing that conference will not settle the problem. The minister has clearly indicated that the United Nations were disorganized and increasingly divided.
As a result of the decision to postpone the UN conference on crime prevention which was to take place in Toronto in the near future, there is another problem. What will happen to the conference on human establishments to be held in Vancouver in 1976? We shall be faced again with the same problem. What will happen in the case of the 1976 Olympic Games in Montreal? It is always the same thing.

The Canadian government assures us that all security precautions will be taken to guarantee the safety of all 1976 Olympic Games participants. Why not take the same security precautions for the conference which will take place in Toronto two months from now? We wonder why, but the issue has been postponed without being solved in any way.
In my opinion, the real problem between the Arab countries and Israel is that of the Palestinian refugees. That is the bone of contention, and as long as their situation is not settled, we shall have difficulties at every level of the United Nations, whether it be in New York, Toronto, Vancouver, Montreal or anywhere in the world. We shall be faced with the same problems, because I think the Arab countries have made up their minds to act through the PLO and succeed where they have failed since 1949.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Secretary General undertook to examine the situation with his legal advisers, and I can understand why. The reason is that the General Assembly, through a resolution, decided to hold the conference in Toronto and named Canada as host. Certainly, in my view, Canada has a role to play in this situation, a role which has to be considered. The Secretary General will communicate to me later in the week the result of his legal studies and we will probably discuss a course of action. We can decide whether to raise the matter before the General Assembly and secure a decision in the General Assembly to postpone the conference until a later date, which is one possibility-or it may be possible to seek a view at the Economic and Social Council of the United Nations which is now in session. It may be possible to secure that view at an early date. It seems to me that pending the clarification of the Secretary General, either of these courses might be justified from the legal point of view.

subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, can the minister tell us if the government has made up its mind to this effect, that no matter what happens in connection with the United Nations, it will not allow this conference to proceed in Canada at present?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I advised the Secretary General that in our opinion, if the conference were held this year in Canada or elsewhere, it would be bound not to succeed in the way it ought to succeed and that Canada would not be prepared to host the conference this year. We would, however, want to hold our position as host and to discharge our international responsibility when circumstances justify the holding of the conference.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two broad conditions which would indicate an easing of the situation that caused us to seek a postponement of this conference. One is the extreme intrusion of unrelated political discussions into what ought to be technical conferences. Mind you, certain of the developing countries feel that these political matters ought to be discussed. It is our view that they ought not to intrude into what are technical conferences. We had a recent example at the conference in Mexico, which in my opinion was damaged because of unrelated political issues entering the discussion. We hope to make some progress in establishing ground rules against the politicization of these conferences. That is one situation.
The other is the expectation that in the meantime there will be a reduction in tensions in the Middle East and that the present unfavourable climate will, if not disappear, be reduced. For example, successful partial negotiations which Secretary Kissinger is presently working on would be a significant development. However, who can predict the future? It is possible that the Geneva talks will be held, the status of the PLO will finally be resolved and we can look to a generally more favourable situation in the Middle East. That is what Canada will be working to achieve in the intervening period.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON HOLDING IN TORONTO UNITED NATIONS CONFERENCE ON PREVENTION OF CRIME

He agreed to that formulation of words. I am

speechtext:
1. (a) (b)
(c) (d)-The new prison industries program referred to in the fact sheet of the Ministry of the Solicitor General dated May 1, 1975 is expected to commence operating in April, 1976. The inmates currently employed in the present industries program number approximately 1,650. The new prison industries program will operate at first on an experimental basis at the Joyceville Institution in Ontario and is likely to employ approximately 80 inmates. The daily rate of pay paid to the 1,650 inmates employed in the present program varies from 70 cents per day to $1,000 per day. The new prison industries program will provide for a pay scale commencing at approximately 60 cents per hour and gradually progress up to the federal minimum wage of $2.20 per hour. The increases in hourly rate will be based on the inmate's performance and production at work. A final decision has not been reached as to the percentage of salary earned to be charged to the participating inmates for their lodgings. However it is expected that this percentage will vary from 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the salary earned.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY CHAIRMEN AND FULL-TIME AND PART-TIME MEMBERS OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as a member of the Special Joint Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service, I rise on third reading to indicate the general acceptance of our party for this important measure. It is, however, an interim measure and the agreement of our party is of an interim nature without prejudice to our position on the final report of the committee which is now studying this matter.
During the various weekends that I am able to spend in my constituency I am finding more and more objections to, and reservations about, the manner in which staff relations in the public service are being regulated. People are fed up with strikes, for example. They are fed up with hold-ups in the mail. There is not a great deal of information that reaches the public in this area except when there is a breakdown of negotiations. This is most unfortunate.
Clearly, one reason for disruptions in the service that the public service is paid to provide, particularly when negotiations for a new contract with Treasury Board are under way, is the failure of the Public Service Staff Relations Board as presently constituted to meet in full the various tasks assigned to it. We have heard from the chairman of that board, an eminent lawyer and specialist in the field of labour relations, Mr. Jacob Finkelman, how the board has found it impossible to resolve employer-employee problems given the present structure of the board.
The board has a number of functions, among the most important of which is to provide rulings on matters that come into dispute between negotiating parties, such as matters of designating confidential exclusion, judgments relating to alleged illegal actions by unions or by management in connection with strikes and lock-outs, and also individual cases in the same areas. There is a further function of arranging, though not necessarily providing, for conciliation and arbitration as required. The calls upon the board have been multiple in the course of time since the board was first instituted in 1957. Mr. Finkelman has drawn to the attention of the special committee that was struck to examine the whole matter just how difficult it is, with a board constituted on a part-time basis, to deal with these many problems.
There was lengthy and amicable discussion in committee since all members of the House, I am happy to say, took a deep interest in the matter and are anxious that the service be provided to the Canadian public in the best manner possible. I pay tribute to all members for their participation and their keenness in questioning; it has been, I think, an exciting and profitable exercise.
However, the Public Service Staff Relations Board, operating on a part-time basis and coming together at the call of the chair once every two or three weeks, say, cannot possibly deal with the dockets before it. For this reason, on hearing the submission of Mr. Finkelman, chairman of the board, the committee decided to ask parliament, on an interim basis, to provide the board with a more permanent status so it could meet regularly, discharge the dockets before it and thereby meet the tasks assigned to it.

July 21, 1975
Public Service
On many occasions the accusation has been made that Treasury Board refuses to negotiate in good faith. This may or may not be. Sometimes it is possibly true; on other occasions it could not be the case. But if the failure of the Public Service Staff Relations Board contributes to this situation because the board is unable to resolve some of the matters before it, thereby preventing one or other of the negotiating parties from coming to terms, then I think it is up to us in this parliament to repair this defect in the PSSRB by giving it the status of permanence and providing it with the equipment to meet its assigned tasks. But again I underline that this is without prejudice to what the special committee should finally decide to do about the whole problem of collective bargaining in the public service.
During the committee proceedings, I contended-and I devoted some time to this also in the House during the budget debate-that somehow or other the public interest must be more deeply involved or vocalized, more deeply articulated, in the negotiation procedure in the public service. After all, in the final analysis it is the public that is the employer. There is a surrogate employer at the moment in the form of Treasury Board, or Treasury Board specialists, but in the final analysis the public is the employer. It pays for the service, it expects the service, and it becomes very annoyed when it does not get the service.
It is my impression that in the special committee in which I participated, that element has not been, yet, fully dealt with. We have not managed, for one reason or another, to ensure that the public interest is fully represented at the bargaining table, as one might say in shorthand. There are not even any proposals before the committee to deal with this question; we are still dealing with it in terms of the present structure-repairing here, making amendments there.
It is my firm intention to make sure that everything is done so that the public is more deeply represented in the negotiating procedures. Any measures or legislative provisions to accomplish that purpose which might run contrary to the legislation now before us will, of course, have to supersede this legislation. That is why I said at the beginning that this is an interim measure. The party to which I belong approves the measure that is being brought forward as an interim measure, conditionally; subject and without prejudice to any further and different sorts of measures that may have to come forward ultimately to deal with this problem.
There is little more that needs to be said at this time, Mr. Speaker. The chairman of the Public Service Staff Relations Board has urged the committee, with all the power in his body, to come forward with some interim relief for the heavy burden now facing the PSSRB, and the measure that was agreed upon in the report and which has now come forward in legislative form will certainly provide that. With the reservations I have already made, I wish to indicate the approval of my party for this measure.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF DEPUTY CHAIRMEN AND FULL-TIME AND PART-TIME MEMBERS OF BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in earlier speeches made on the subject of this bill, members of the New Democratic Party have made it clear

that we support the purpose of this legislation. The bill would restructure the Public Service Staff Relations Board so that it can cope more adequately with the pile-up of disputes, certifications and adjudication of problems. We support a measure that would tend to ameliorate this build-up.
However, the act being amended by this bill deals with the very important question of the collective bargaining rights of civil servants. Indeed, the Public Service Staff Relations Board itself is inextricably involved in a current and symbolically important dispute which I should like to take a few minutes to discuss this afternoon, namely, the suspension of Mr. Arthur Stewart, president of the 8,000-member Supply and Services union. Mr. Stewart is an elected head of a union representing a significant number of civil servants. I wish to spend a few minutes on this important case because crucial questions of principle have been raised on the matter by the minister who is directly responsible, the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Goyer) and by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
I hope at the conclusion of my remarks, which deliberately will be kept brief, the minister responsible for this bill will reply and make clear what I consider to be the ambiguous position of the government in respect of the rights of civil servants arising from the Arthur Stewart case. Mr. Stewart, Mr. Speaker and members of the House will recall, was suspended for making certain public criticisms of the department in which he worked, the Department of Supply and Services. While he worked in that department he was also the head of a union.
The public criticism that Mr. Stewart made of his department can be broken into two elements. One is that he was critical of the labour relations which existed within the department and which currently exist within the department. The other is that he criticized the hiring within the department of too many senior management people. In his public criticism which took the form of an article published by the Ottawa Citizen, Mr. Stewart did reach explicit connections between what he regarded as faulty labour relations, on the one hand, and inappropriate hiring of too many management personnel, on the other, and the minister. In other words, there was an explicit connection made by Mr. Stewart between what he considered bad administration by the department and the minister's responsibility.
I wish to make essentially two points on this. First, the kind of public criticisms made by Mr. Stewart of his department were essentially administrative in nature. That seems to me to be of fundamental importance in this case. Second, such criticisms made by Mr. Stewart, as a trade union representative, ought not only to be his right but also his obligation if he is effectively to do his job as a representative of the working people in that department. If that is the case, then what possible justification could there be for his suspension?
He was suspended for three months without pay. That constitutes a reduction of his income by 25 per cent for one year. It is not a trivial matter in terms of his personal subsistence, but quite apart from that an important matter of principle is at stake here. What grounds would justify Mr. Stewart's suspension? One which we must reject outright, of course, is that attributed to the Minister of
July 21, 1975

Supply and Services who was quoted by the press as saying he would be prepared to accept criticism from his peers but not from an employee. That kind of position, I hope, would not be accepted by members of any party on either side of the House. I would hope that upon reflection the Minister of Supply and Services would agree that he overstated his case. Certainly I hope it is an overstatement for a minister of the Crown to say that no form of criticism is to be justified except from his peers.
A different kind of justification was offered for the suspension of Mr. Stewart by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister prefaced his comment in the House, in reply to the questions put by me last week, by saying that he did not have the details of the case. However, not having the details of the case did not prohibit his reaching what he regards as a profound conclusion. He went on to say that he shared the minister's judgment that Mr. Stewart ought to have been suspended because he was making political criticism. If hon. members would check Hansard, they would find that the Prime Minister took that position. When pursued, in subsequent question periods, by myself about what is the definition of "political criticism", the Prime Minister offered no answer, relying-as he does quite frequently-on rhetorical responses in an effort to deal with the issue by not facing it at all.
I say, in all seriousness, that the issue is of great importance. If the Prime Minister is to say that the kind of criticism made by Mr. Stewart as a trade union official of the department constitutes political criticism, the only conclusion one can draw from that is that any criticism made by an employee or trade union official would constitute political criticism. If a trade unionist criticizes the internal functioning of a department on an administrative basis, as was done by Mr. Stewart-which has been said by the Prime Minister to be political-then I suggest that, surely, criticism about wage levels within a department in the course of bargaining in private or in public would also be political criticism. Questions about the number of hours of work within a department would also constitute political criticism. A member opposite says that is nonsense. I should like to ask him why it is nonsense.
The negotiators for the packinghouse workers, for the steelworkers and for the UAW, to name three unions in Canada, do not hesitate to criticize the internal administrative operations of corporations with whom they are negotiating, because when speaking for the employees they represent-whether in corporations or departments- union members have a legitimate interest in the whole functioning of either the private corporation or the government department. They feel as employees they have a basic obligation to make suggestions about improvements in a firm or department. Surely, since we permit such rights, without anyone seriously questioning them, to exist for trade union people in the private sector, we should permit them as well in the public sector for a representative of the employees to speak on their behalf and to make internal criticisms.
The second reason, apart from trying to improve the functioning of the private corporation or the internal operations of the department, is the more immediate point which is made frequently, that if you administer your
Public Service
department better, as a result you can perhaps get better pay for your employees. It is not an entirely unique situation for trade union negotiators to suggest that by clearing management waste a company will be able to pay employees a little better. That is another purpose for making the kind of criticism that Mr. Stewart made of the Minister of Supply and Services. Again, I would like to know why that should be stopped and why not only Mr. Stewart but now, by implication, any union official in the civil service will be curtailed in making such statements.
I say that if that is the position of the government, then what this case amounts to is a significant intimidation of all civil servants employed by the federal government, because what the federal government is saying is that if you have an effective spokesman representing you and making criticisms of the department, then that spokesman runs the very serious risk of losing his job, or at least of losing it for a good part of the year. How could you develop a more inhibiting kind of procedure than to tell the people who are negotiating with the government that if they get tough with their negotiations, if they are really serious about them, they may lose their jobs? I hope that the Prime Minister simply overstated his case, as he does on occasion in the House in reply to questions, and that in the final analysis he does not regard the kind of criticism made by Mr. Stewart as the kind that warrants a suspension. I would like to hear the minister clarify that situation this afternoon in winding up the debate on this bill which, as I said earlier, we support.
I think it is of basic importance that the people elected by the civil servants of Canada to represent them should be free, in terms of the range of topics they can raise in criticism of the minister heading the department or officials working under that minister. To restrict their freedom of action along the lines stated by the Minister of Supply and Services, and along the even broader lines indicated by the Prime Minister, will seriously inhibit their effectiveness in terms of doing the job for which they were elected by the civil servants, namely, good bargaining with the government.
Before I sit down I want to point out, as I did in the question period, that even if one allows, as I do not, that the kind of criticism made by Mr. Stewart is political, surely the punishment handed out by the government is away out of line in terms of what would be justified by any sense of decency or equity. Just compare the situation of Mr. Stewart with that of Admiral Boyle in the navy on the east coast of Canada when he spoke to the Conservative Party caucus on the defence policy. As an admiral in the navy, he spoke to a political party in explicit criticism of the government's policy. Nothing could be more political than the kind of statement that Admiral Boyle made, and nothing could be more appropriate than the government's response, which was to point out that no admiral or other official of the Department of National Defence should have the right publicly to criticize the defence policy of the Crown.
I agreed with the government's position in that instance and I agree that policy statements constitute political criticism. But compare the punishment handed out to Admiral Boyle with that handed out to Mr. Stewart. Mr. Stewart, a man with considerably less income and consid-

July 21, 1975

erably less influence in the government, is suspended for three months, with loss of income, while Admiral Boyle- who makes explicit political criticism-is brought to Ottawa for a little chit-chat with the minister. As the minister pointed out, no doubt his actions were wrong. But that is all that was done. He was sent back to the east coast and told not to speak to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) and those Conservative fellows again in that way, because it was out of order for an admiral in the Canadian navy to so act. We agree with that, but what we do not agree with is a government that interprets the administrative criticism of another employee as a political act and then takes away that man's income for three months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief on this matter. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) spoke about the situation with regard to the criticism of the government by a civil servant, a matter which was first raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). I intervened, in the form of a question supplementary to those asked by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. Because this is a subject in which I am quite interested, and because we are wrestling with this sort of thing in a joint committee at present, I want to say that there are, obviously, certain areas where those who are advisers to the government and in close contact with it must have some inhibition with regard to their open criticism, though I do not think we need to define them at this time.
However, I want to say that one of the reasons civil servants of this government are driven, from time to time, to indulge in open criticism, and occasionally to see that documents within the possession of the departments are sometimes provided surreptitiously to the press and to the public, is the inherent penchant of this government for obsessive secrecy.
The test is when a civil servant sees that if the document or the information which is essential to be released for the good of the public, for the welfare of the country and for the good of parliament, is released, he or she would be in a difficult position. True enough, his responsibility as a civil servant may compel him to say to himself that he should not do this, but as a citizen of this country he has a certain responsibility with regard to the decisions which are made in parliament and to information which should come to the public. I think that is the kind of test where at present, unfortunately, civil servants are limited.

I know that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp)-and I give him and members of the committee credit for it-seems to have some knowledge of that. They have not gone as far as I want them to go. It may well be that they may go further. But the document I asked about today, concerning a very important issue, is one which the country and parliament should have had provided for it when we were involved in the debates last winter in connection with energy matters.
According to the press, we now find that there was in the possession of the government six or seven months ago a document with regard to the very critical situation in the supply and the potential supply of natural gas. That information, if it was in the possession of the government-and that has not been denied today-should have been made public and should have been made available to members of this House for the purpose of the debate which was then taking place. If it was as essential as I deem it could have been, it may well be that a civil servant, despite his relationship with the government, might have been justified in releasing it.
My seatmate once had the honour to be premier of the province of Nova Scotia, and the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) was once premier of the province of Saskatchewan. I imagine they must have had certain rules with regard to information; no government can operate on the basis that everything which comes into the possession of a civil servant must be released. The case of Mr. Stewart has been referred to by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby. It forcibly points out the need to engage in the adoption of certain rules which will probably make it unnecessary for that kind of action to be repeated.
Some hon. members may have been observing the very interesting case in the United Kingdom where the diaries of the late Richard Crossman are now the subject of legal action. The late Mr. Crossman, a very distinguished member of the Labour cabinet whom I had the pleasure of meeting both here and in the United Kingdom, who was also Lord Privy Seal, government House leader and quite a scholar, left diaries with regard to his operations within the Labour Party and the Labour government. I think those diaries were vetted, so far as matters of national security were concerned and those parts which were sensitive within the public domain, and about a quarter of the diaries was published in the London Times.
There was then a proposal to publish them in book form, but the prime minister, Mr. Harold Wilson, the leader of the socialist Labour Party in the United Kingdom, issued instructions to his attorney general, Mr. Silkin, to secure an injunction prohibiting the publication of those papers on the ground that they were inimical to the public interest. As a matter of fact, knowledgeable journalists and political scientists who observed the material in those documents have come to the conclusion that they simply showed ordinary, fallible men making grievous errors and operating in darkness or near darkness in connection with the affairs of government.
They also showed that in many respects the affairs of the country were being run by senior civil servants and
July 21, 1975

that the members of the Labour cabinet only gave their consent to proposals brought to them. I am not going to deal with that matter because I hope it will come up in subsequent debates, but I point it out to indicate to this House that, hopefully, this fall we may have an opportunity to discuss the extent to which material within the possession of a government should be kept secret or should be made public. If the House, as I hope it will, comes to the right decision, then we will find that it will not be necessary for people like Mr. Stewart, who obviously felt he was fulfilling a public obligation by making known these facts, to be faced with the very difficult decision which he had to make in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to begin by commending the work of the joint committee which considered this bill and which originally made the recommendations upon which it is based. Several hon. members have commended the work of that committee. I had the privilege of appearing before it as a witness, and there I found a spirit of co-operation which I wish prevailed more generally in this House. It has done a commendable piece of work. I hope the committee will continue its work and that in due course we will have a report on the more substantive matters which are before it.
It seems to me that most of the debate on third reading has been a little irrelevant to the bill itself. However, let me make some brief comments on the speeches made by the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) and by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin). If I may begin with my friend the Conservative House leader, he and I have had many discussions about the question of secrecy in government. I do not quite know how it got into this debate, but here it is. I speak now not only as a minister and a member of parliament but as a former civil servant who saw the problem from the other side.
Some hon. members may recall that I was the centre of a controversy about the publication of a government document of which I happened to be the signatory, namely, the famous hidden report which the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) brandished about the country in the general election of 1958.

speechtext: The House resumed, from Friday, July 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-66, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 7416).

Mr. Speaker, in supporting our amendment that this bill be not now read the second time, I am pleased to do so to emphasize that there are many good reasons for making this very reasonable suggestion. The measures contained in Bill C-66 are, for the most part, poorly advised. They are not going to do the job and have the economic results that the minister anticipated. For the most part, I fail to see the urgency that the government has particularly emphasized lately, because it may very well be that section 17 of the Financial Administration Act would make the part of the legislation relating to the rebate provision irrelevant. The relevant section reads:

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
The governor in council, on the recommendation of the Treasury Board, whenever he considers it in the public interest, may remit any tax, fee or penalty.
It may be argued that this only applies to taxes which are in place but I suggest, with deference, that if there is no tax legislation in place, then there is a very good argument to be made that you do not need a bill to authorize the rebate in these circumstances either. Even though the measures contained in Bill C-66 result from the budget, they ought not to be proceeded with too quickly- particularly the ten-cent tax on gasoline-until proper administrative procedures for processing the tax are put in place.
It would have been preferable if the minister had made arrangements-even if there had to be lengthy discussions beforehand to make this more practicable-to withhold the imposition of this tax until parliament had given its sanction. I realize there are some difficulties in this suggestion, but it worries me, as a member, to see another situation where the people of Canada are faced with a very regressive tax being collected without the legislative sanction of the House of Commons. I think this is a very poor precedent. If the principle were extended to the point where the omnibus bill which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) intends to bring in with regard to criminal law were to be enforced now, and we were asked as members to approve it later, there would be a great outcry in the country. I think you can draw a fair analogy between what the Parliament of Canada is being asked to do here and what could be the case in the future if this sort of thing were allowed to continue.
I should like to say a few things with reference to the proposed increase in the air transportation tax and come back to the famous, or infamous ten-cent tax in a few moments. The proposed increase in the air transportation tax is another regressive and counterproductive move. No less a person than the president of the Air Transport Association of Canada recently had this to say:
Members of our association, travel agents and charters are concerned about the application of the increased rate for air transportation tax effective August 1 if it will require adjustment and collections from travellers who have bought air transportation before the first of August.
Here is another unfortunate complication from proceeding in this precipitous way. He continued:
Such adjustments and collections at airports at time of departure during the heavy travel season would be irritating, disruptive and lead to serious criticism of the agents, carriers and government.
The minister proposed to raise the air transportation tax limits substantially from the levels imposed by the existing legislation, that is clear. I understand this increase is designed to generate another $16 million of revenue in this fiscal year, added to a ticket tax revenue take of $53 million, so that this would amount to a total annual revenue of approximately $69 million.
Far better for the government, in the name of restraint, to have cut back on some of the gigantic sums which have been appropriated for airport expansion, such as Pickering, which the majority of the people affected do not want, and Mirabel which does not, as yet, have the proper supporting infrastructure. It therefore could very easily have some of its budgetary appropriations deferred until such time as the lack of adequate road infrastructure is over-

come, particularly since knowledgeable people are well aware that the airport at Dorval has not yet been used to its full potential. The lack of adequate road infrastructure is nothing short of a catastrophe. Quebec has been delaying the road service due to a siphoning of funds to buttress the Olympics. Ottawa did a poor job of future planning and should have anticipated what was likely to happen.
Weekend flights will be the biggest problem, since the Autoroute will be congested with people heading north from Montreal to the Laurentians in the summer for holidays and in the winter for skiing. The trip from Montreal to Mirabel is expected to take two hours, and certainly passengers will have to leave earlier to catch a flight to Mirabel as compared to Dorval under present circumstances.
The Air Transport Association of Canada makes the point that the latest increase appears to further discriminate against those who prefer to travel by air, since similar taxes were not imposed on people using other forms of transportation. It has already been pointed out to the Minister of Transport by knowledgeable people in the Air Transport Association of Canada that people living in cities or towns some distance from the point where charter flights begin sometimes find themselves paying a second airport tax because they have to pay the tax on the connecting flight to the charter flight, as well as another tax on the charter flight.
Certainly, the tax should also apply to foreign travellers using Canadian airports, which is not the case at the moment since the tax applies only to people boarding flights originating in Canada. The whole concept, as usual, has been poorly thought-out. It would do no harm if it and the tax increase were to be delayed until some further thought could be given to the entire matter.
Coming back to the ten-cent gasoline tax, it is particularly damaging to people in my constituency who have to travel long distances to search for and to find employment. It is wrong in still another way for provinces such as Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island which are isolated geographically and in the sense of energy availability. This ten-cent tax, coming upon the $1.50 per barrel increase, imposes what amounts to an unnatural cost and burden on those provinces compared to Ontario, where about 50 per cent of the energy requirements are available from hydro. Prince Edward Island, for example, has to rely on energy obtained from petroleum products for nearly 100 per cent, of its energy requirements at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, I think the minister did something that was even more regressive than he intended by imposing the ten-cent tax. He has done an extraordinary thing; he has brought in a two-price system based not on geography but on class distinction. I say this because whether one pays the tax or not will depend upon who one is. If a person can bring himself within an exclusion by pleading his profession or other circumstances, such as business requirements, then he is able to escape. For the most part, those able to escape will be those who can afford to pay the tax, and those who are least able to afford it will have to pay. That in itself is an excellent reason for the minister to take another look at this.
July 21, 1975

In the measures arising out of the budget, the Minister of Finance was required to make some hard choices. He was restricted in his options because of the economic climate-not the meteorological one upon which he was inclined to call at times-which he and this government helped to create by policies in previous budgets and the implementation of measures in past years. In many respects I feel sympathetic toward the minister, but my sympathy is tempered by recollections of his past behaviour. If the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) was too honest and direct for the advancement of his own political cause in telling Canadians the truth a year ago, and offering a realistic assessment of the consequences of unrestrained and undisciplined economic behaviour, the same cannot be said about the conduct of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Can you imagine a measure like this being brought in by the government before the last election? I suggest that no one in his right mind would even consider the possibility. To the credit of the Leader of the Opposition, if he felt that a measure like this was necessary, without doubt he would bring it in at anytime, but he would never bring in an ill-advised measure like this. The Leader of the Opposition offered Canadians the alternative of economic medicine which might have been bitter for a while, as most medicines are. The Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister preferred to offer Canadians champagne and optimism, assuring Canadians just over one year ago that all was well with the economy and the nation and that the Tories were preaching gloom and doom without just cause.
The government made promises, many promises: a glowing new transportation policy was to be implemented immediately; there was to be an end to regional wage disparities. Liberal candidates in the Atlantic provinces emphasized this particular election promise and said they were behind it. We now see its results! Frankly, I do not have time in the brief time allocated to me to list all the promises made. Now, after the champagne days of last summer, after the broken promises, comes the inevitable letdown and hangover. No one deserves it more than the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: The minister brought in good policies.

No one will bear the brunt of it, as the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) knows, more than the Minister of Finance. The glory days of the Minister of Finance are over and if he is not careful he may fit the description which the immortal Winston Churchill used when referring to Lord Roseberry several decades ago. Sir Winston described him as having outlived his future by ten years and his past by more than 20.
Time passes quickly and these tax measures may mark the beginning of the end of the Minister of Finance's adroit ability to avoid well deserved political flack. Henceforth, he and the government will be in a great deal of trouble. No one has earned this trouble more than the government. True, the budget did pay lip service to restraint, which is good; it also made the gesture of helping people holding Canadian government annuities. That
Excise Tax Act
was a humanitarian move, as those people had been most unfairly affected by the government's policies which incurred unrestrained inflation.
With the exception of a few tangible measures like the ones just mentioned, the budget is not innovative nor imaginative. Measures like this one fail to recognize that the different regions of this country are constantly encountering different economic difficulties. A policy that is good for one part of the country, as has been said many times, may be the very worst policy for another. In one region unemployment and stagnation may be the major problem, but in another the economy may be booming and inflation may be the biggest problem. Although economic theory dictates different solutions for each different problem, our political and financial system is such-this has been true no matter what government has been in power- that only one national fiscal policy is arrived at. It is imposed on the nation as a whole, despite our great differences and regional anomalies.
Politics dictates, apparently, that fiscal policy should be aimed at solving the problems of the most heavily populated and financially important regions, which means central Canada. As I said at the outset, this particular tax will make its greatest impact felt on those regions of the country which can least afford to pay it, and on those individuals who can least afford it. The other regions of the country are left to get along as well as possible with a fiscal policy which may not suit their economic situation.
I therefore expected the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) at least to pay lip service to the idea of a flexible fiscal policy. Why not develop a flexible policy which will take into account the regional differences in our country? More specifically, Mr. Speaker, at this moment why could the government not introduce a regional fiscal policy which could make a special effort to stimulate the economy of the maritimes by providing money at low interest to small businesses?
The usual criticisms of such suggested policies are well known. Those who criticize say that capital investment will go to the area where the best return on the money lent can be obtained, that is, it will go to where interest rates are highest. Thus, if interest rates are higher in central Canada but lower in the other regions, the banks will do most of their business in the high interest area. This activity will lead to the opposite of what one would wish to achieve by having different interest rates in different areas.
The government has never been reluctant to interfere with and modify the unrestrained policies of private enterprise. This is not necessarily bad. For the sake of argument, why not make it mandatory for the large financial institutions to lend a certain amount of money at low interest to small businesses in depressed regions? True, this would tamper to some extent with the freedom of our banking system, but the government has willingly tampered with the system in the past. Why not experiment in this regard? Even if interest rates must be subsidized to a certain extent, it would be worth while seeing how such an experimental program works. Depressed regions could well be more quickly developed if we used this method. The program would alleviate, if successful, the constant

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
drain of taxpayers' money going to the depressed regions. This money which is channelled into the areas through DREE, UIC, cost-sharing programs, etc., might not be needed to such an extent if this program were introduced and great savings could be effected in the long run.
As for needing to maintain high interest rates in Canada because world interest rates are high and Canada having to offer a good return to attract sufficient investment to counter our trade deficit, is there not some way of adopting a two-price system of interest rates, one for the domestic Canadian market and another for outside financiers from whom we try to borrow?
Although the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion said before the budget was brought down that he would provide direct input into the budget and put forward recommendations concerning DREE, which has an important role to play in this country, the budget did not deal with DREE. Neither in the budget nor in Bill C-66 is there evidence to show that the minister tried to do anything to counter the impact which the government's unfair measures will have on those regions of the country for which he is responsible. It was disappointing to see that DREE was not given higher priority. We should be thankful for small mercies. No DREE programs were cut back and for this we give the government credit.
I expected the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion to say something innovative and different when he spoke in the recent budget debate. His speech disappointed me, not because he did not speak well-he always does-and not because it was not entertaining.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: It made sense.

It was a defensive speech. There are ministers on the treasury benches, as the member for St. Boniface no doubt realizes, who are simply incapable of formulating good policy. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion is not one of those. If he were allowed to give his talents full rein, I am sure he would produce better policies than some of his colleagues are producing. Being concerned about what might happen to my province, I asked the minister the following question on June 11, as recorded on page 6649 of Hansard
Because of continuing high unemployment and other economic difficulties, particularly in the Atlantic region, can the minister say whether any specific arrangements will be incorporated into the budget on his recommendations specifically designed to assist DREE to cope better with economic disparities. I am thinking of some measures to single out regions covered by his department for new initiatives in terms of economic assistance to cope with the real difficulties that we have not been able to eradicate. Will the minister be making a statement on this?
The minister declined to make a statement, but said:
-I am sure the hon. member appreciates that while it is true I will be making recommendations and suggestions with regard to certain budgetary matters, the outcome will only be known on budget night.
The folly of this proposed tax must be apparent to all. Obviously, the minister, despite his well-meaning effort to influence his less sensitive colleagues, was not able to do anything to help the depressed areas of Canada improve the significantly poorer position they will find themselves in as a result of the passage of bills like Bill C-66.

I am sure that in the province represented by the hon. member for St. Boniface there are areas where people are drawing unemployment insurance and there are sometimes cases which come to his attention where the person involved is expected to drive a long distance in order to obtain employment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Not in my constituency.

Well, if that is not the case with the hon. member for St. Boniface, I want to tell him and the House it is a very common occurrence in my constituency in Nova Scotia, particularly in the area known as the eastern shore where there are very few opportunities for employment. It becomes a case of real economic difficulty and puzzlement in deciding whether a person applying for unemployment insurance has made enough of an effort over a wide enough area, even keeping in mind the limited opportunities available for employment.
When a person is expected to drive 50 or 60 miles from the eastern shore of Nova Scotia to the Halifax-Dartmouth area, or to Truro or New Glasgow where there is a greater population and where there are greater and more varied opportunities for employment, it is a very dicey situation. Does it pay to drive 40 or 50 miles? If such a person has to drive this distance-and it is quite common that they do- the hon. member can appreciate the dilemma in which such a person finds himself. If he has to pay an extra ten cents a gallon, with a very marginal job and no hope whatsoever of any rebate, this inflicts a very real hardship. The government and the Minister of Finance should be aware of this. They ought to take measures that will somehow alleviate this problem.
Even in an energy short era, I fail to see how this tax will promote conservation. Frankly, in most cases there is no alternative to the car for people to get to work. If the only purpose of this tax is to generate revenue, rather than to conserve, I say that it is a very regressive measure and ought not to be proceeded with. If the revenue derived from this tax were to be specifically channelled into the development of coal in Nova Scotia, for example, which would provide an alternate energy source, or some sort of public transportation system to help those who have to travel long distances, there would be a little more sympathy for it; but it does not do anything in this regard.
I do not know on how great an authority it is, but from some publications I have been reading lately I am led to believe there is a good possibility that in the years to come our uranium reserves may be depleted to the point where Canada will be faced with a situation with regard to uranium such as the one we now face with our petroleum. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) has assured us that this is not the case. He said that he will be looking into this matter and will take whatever additional measures are necessary to protect the long-term interests of this country. I certainly hope that is the case. It would be ironic if in 20 years, as an official of the Ontario Energy Research Board has stated, Canada were in the position with respect to our uranium reserves that we are now in with regard to petroleum.
July 21, 1975

I hope the government will take a sober second look at what it is doing. It does not seem right that the people of this country should be subjected to a tax which is obviously inflationary.
Hear, hear!

As I say, I remain to be convinced that this measure has any merit to encourage conservation. The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) is a conservationist. He knows very well that this tax will not do anything productive.
You are right.

It will only exarcerbate the differences between those Canadians able to afford the good life and those who cannot afford to live well. If there is one thing the average.person in this automobile-oriented society will do, it will be to hang on to and drive his automobile even to the point, in some cases, of skimping on food for his family. Members opposite know that is the case, particularly where there is no alternate means of transportation. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) seriously to consider the consequences of going ahead with this bill in its present form, particularly when the government is so poorly organized to administer the effects of the tax.
It is significant that no cabinet ministers have risen to support the Minister of Finance on this. I am waiting to hear the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford) state the clear and unequivocal tax policy that will be put into effect with regard to the rebate. I await with interest to hear what the minister's other colleagues have to say. I hope that by their silence they have not committed themselves to going ahead with this measure in its present form. After all, the PLO decision was put off, so this government can change its mind!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow a question?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That can only be done with the permission of the hon. member. Does the hon. member agree?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, has the hon. member discussed the program he is speaking of with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson)? Has he done any research with regard to the benefits his province has received through the DREE program? I understand from what he has said that he does not know the benefits his province received through that particular minister and program.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer the hon. member for St. Boniface by saying that the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and I have had many discussions about the economic problems that face not only Nova Scotia but the other provinces. I am well aware of the substantial sums which this government has diverted into this part of Canada. However, in relative terms, I remind the hon. member that all the money that has been diverted into Atlantic Canada for regional eco-
Excise Tax Act
nomic expansion in terms of incentive grants is substantially less than the proposed costs of either of the monster airports at Pickering or Mirabel.
