speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Turner (Ottawa-Carleton) that Bill C-66, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole; and the amendment thereto of Mr. Stanfield (p. 7416).

Mr. Speaker, I wish to open by saying that I am very much in agreement with a great deal of what has been said by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). I understand that his part of the country, along with other parts, has special difficulties. I want to assure him that this particular bill strikes a grievous blow at many people in the central provinces as well. I refer particularly to constituencies such as my own of Greenwood. I will discuss that in a little more detail later.
I should like to make it clear from the beginning that I do not intend to take up the full 40 minutes allotted to me. I am strongly of the opinion that except in special cases, that is too much time. I think we make much better speeches when we are confined to 20 minutes. This being my view, I should like to be consistent with it and try to keep my own speech short; I do not always succeed, but I hope I shall on this occasion.
In my previous incarnation I was connected with the legal profession, and had I been called upon to give judgment on Bill C-66 I would have dealt with it very quickly;

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
I would have been content to say I concurred with my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent) and others who have spoken, especially the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes), and that I had nothing to add. However, I am not speaking in a judicial capacity; I am here as a representative of my constituents. I say that this tax has dealt a grievous blow to them, and I believe I owe it to the people I represent to express the strongly held views they hold on this legislation.
To put the matter in a nutshell or, possibly, in one or two nutshells, this tax is, in my view, inflationary, regressive and unjust. I do not intend to expand on the inflationary and regressive aspects since something which is inflationary and regressive is inherently unjust. The reason it is unjust is simple: it imposes a burden on those least able to bear it, factory and office workers for whom a car is a necessity, not a luxury, because they have to travel to work. It is these people who will bear the major burden of the tax, not the well-to-do, not those who use cars for pleasure or as a luxury.
There are many thousands in the riding of Greenwood who use their cars to get to work. We have heard from people in other parts of the country about this problem, and it exists in my area. In a large urban area such as I represent, a great many people do not work near where they live. It is by no means uncommon for people to travel 25 miles to work and back again, sometimes more, sometimes less; I think 25 miles would be a reasonable average. This is the group which has to bear the main burden of the new tax.
The action of the government in this regard illustrates as well as anything could the difference between the Liberal Party and the New Democratic Party. The tax system favoured by the Liberals is tilted in favour of the rich. The philosophy of the NDP, on the other hand, is egalitarian. We believe in taxes such as steeply graded income taxes which seek to create a more just society by equalizing incomes.
During the course of the present debate, one of the members who supports the government, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin), said it was better to impose the tax on the people who consume the product rather than have it paid by way of general taxation which, however imperfectly, is so set up at the present time that heavier burdens are placed on the well-to-do. It is precisely this which distinguishes our party from that of the government on this matter. He said the middle income groups would prefer this way of doing things, rather than in the form of income tax which, he added, falls particularly heavily on middle income groups.
I do not think the income tax bears so terribly hard on those groups, but it certainly does not bear with undue harshness on the affluent. It is all very well to talk as the Liberal Party does from time to time about the just society, but unless the taxation system is directed to creating the just society by bringing about a more equal share of the national income, the phrase "just society" becomes an example of nothing more than election-time rhetoric.
The bill we are debating is another example of the direction the government's policies are taking. It is designed to bolster up an acquisitive society with all its inequities. There is another area in which the measure

would fall hardest on those with modest means. The hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie has explained how at certain levels of society the automobile is used extensively for vacation travel. The advent of this tax will force many people to revise their summer vacation travel plans. This, of course, will hit hard those who depend on tourism for their income. But there is another group which will be affected. There is one reform which has come about in the lifestyle of Canadians during my lifetime and during my active interest in politics which I most heartily support. It is the tremendous growth of vacations with pay.
In the thirties, when I first took an active interest in politics, visiting the beautiful lakes and rivers with which Canada is so richly endowed was the privilege of the affluent few. Very few industrial workers got a vacation unless, of course, they had one forced upon them by prolonged unemployment. Fortunately, collective bargaining and legislation together have changed all this, and today many workers have been able to acquire or rent summer cottages where they can spend weekends or vacations using, in most cases, their own cars for transport.
I am afraid this bill will make it harder for these people to afford a healthy and enjoyable experience which in my view is the birthright of all Canadians, especially of industrial workers and their families, that of getting out of the cities into the open where they can benefit their health and sustain their spirits by recreation.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has expressed the hope that the excise tax, combined with the expected increase in the price of a barrel of oil, will encourage motorists to save gasoline. In other words, the conservation of gasoline, a highly desirable objective, is called in aid in an effort to justify this tax. But where is the evidence that the effect of the legislation will be to save gasoline? If saving gas is the objective, there are many, far better ways in which it could be accomplished. One would be to negotiate with the provinces to bring about a reduction of the speed limit. Incidentally, this might save a few lives as well. If the government were concerned about the conservation of gasoline, it would move in the field of extending public transit systems which today are only a supplement, not an alternative, to travel by car.
Above all, if the government were to carry out the promises made in the last election, it would transform this situation. Let me put on the record some of the things that were promised in the last election campaign. On June 17, 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced in Toronto a $270 million program to aid public transit. He said:
A liberal government would pay 100 per cent of the cost of Canadian-made commuter vehicles and 50 per cent of the cost of platforms and stations. The government would also pay 25 per cent of the cost of Canadian-manufactured vehicles for public transit within cities. Encouragement and assistance would be given to smaller municipalities in the creation of new transit systems, Canadian industry would be encouraged to develop passenger vehicles, and experimentation with new transit systems would be assisted by federal financing of demonstration projects.
On the next day, June 18, while in Cornwall, the Prime Minister said:
July 21, 1975

-a Liberal government would take responsibility for rail passenger service out of the hands of Canadian National and Canadian Pacific railways and entrust the task to a new Crown corporation. The corporation would run high-speed rail services in heavily populated areas such as Windsor-Quebec City corridor, introduce luxurious transcontinental excursion trains and establish a "super-bus" service between medium sized cities.
Incidentally, while I am reciting the promises that were made, may I point out that the Liberals also promised to set up a national urban transportation development corporation to promote improvements and develop policy on urban transportation. This was mentioned in the 1973-74 annual report of the Ministry of State for Urban Affairs. But on May 1, 1975, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) admitted that the corporation had not yet been set up. All this talk during the election campaign has turned out to be mere promises designed for election purposes. But its relevancy to this discussion is very real, because if these promises were implemented it would take the pressure off the necessity of travelling by automobile and would in fact conserve gasoline.
The government's actions speak louder than its words. We have already had a reference in the House this afternoon to the Pickering airport. If it were constructed, it would serve roughly 10 per cent of the public, a small section. If it were constructed, it would gobble up high-class agricultural land. If it were constructed, it would multiply the transportation problems of urban areas such as my own riding. No one really wants this new airport. There has never been any demonstrated need for it. Public opinions polls have been taken in the area affected and have shown fairly substantial majorities against it. I do not know which members the government has consulted, but whenever it consulted me I made it very clear that the people of Greenwood do not want the Pickering airport.
If the proposed airport were built as a single runway, minimum airport, it would divert fewer than 10 per cent of aircraft operations from Malton by 1980-and this was supposed to be the purpose of the new airport. It appears that plans have been silently switched again and we are now back to a large Pickering airport. Only the refusal of the Ontario government to provide the highways and infrastructure has caused the government to halt its obstinate course.
Let the government take this ill-conceived scheme and drop it in the lake. Let it use the money to carry out its promise of a rapid transit development system within and between cities. Although the Minister of Finance is not here this afternoon-he usually is, but I assume he will read the debate-I suggest that his budget and taxation policy be used to implement, not to disregard, the promises made in the election campaign which are beneficial to the people.
Can anyone wonder at the apathy and cynicism with which much of our political system is regarded by the public? In my view, this is a bad bill, and in saying that I feel I am expressing the feelings of the vast majority of my constituents. I condemn this particular bill and I make it clear that I, for one-and, indeed, I think all members of my party-will vote against it.
Excise Tax Act

Mr. Speaker, in rising on Bill C-66 and the amendment of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), I have definitely no intention of extending this debate which, in my opinion, has been dragging on for quite enough time. In fact, you know about that from what we did during the week-end. We kept hoping it would be over, but as there seems to be no end to that debate, everyone has to say his word, and I realize government members are doing everything they can to restrict that debate, but I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, we are heading for a marathon type debate on that bill which will make a complete mess of the well deserved vacation of all members.
Considering the number of members who want to speak and who will, it is obvious that Progressive Conservative members definitely want to drag this session throughout summer.
I have once again to criticize the government, because it is always the same thing, the same tactics. They always take advantage of the fact that the session is coming to an end, or that a vacation is getting nearer to introduce controversial bills like this one. Of course, this bill is a logical consequence of the last budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), a budget which we actually turn down.
After wasting so much time in this House with empty speeches throughout the winter months, as soon as the few sunny days of summer are back, the government forces us to do everything in double quick time if we are to get some vacation. Mr. Speaker, it is childish, ridiculous and unfair, not only to members of parliament, but also to their families who are waiting for them to come back and spend a few days in the sun. Let us not forget that in autumn and during the long winter months, once again, we shall have plenty of time to make speeches and talk to the Chair. I therefore urge Progressive Conservative members, even though they are like us convinced that that tax is unfair, to have some pity for all those children who are waiting for us to be back for a few weeks. If this debate was to have a positive outcome, I would be the first one to stay here all summer, but as we all know, the government has an absolute majority, and everything will end up in a vote which will once again ratify the government's proposals. This government was elected by the people, and this is a democracy!
Hear, hear!

We are of course opposed to Bill C-66 which levies a 10 cent excise tax on every gallon of gas used for private purposes. For the information of the public, I must say that this tax does not result from the increase in oil prices. I do not know whether the mass media or the government itself led the people to believe that this 10 cent markup was due to the increase in oil prices, because this was the general impression among the people. I spent the whole weekend trying to explain that it was not as a result of the increase in oil prices. They will experience the result in a few weeks, but this is an excise tax, a 10 cent tax per gallon of gas.
7778

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
Mr. Speaker, actually the increase in oil prices has nothing to do with the 10 cent tax per gallon. This bill stems from a tax, once again, an excise tax of 10 cents a gallon on gas that could have been imposed on any other produce, for that matter. So, I feel it is most unfortunate that gas should have been singled out to collect budgetary funds after the spiralling increase faced by the people in recent weeks. Why, for example, has the tax on wines not been maintained? They went as far as removing the tax on wines; why did they not tax alcohol, tobacco even more? Let us levy if necessary a tax on luxury items but let us stop taking from those who are in immediate need of a commodity, gas for example, those who must use it to go to work.
Our opposition is still stronger as far as selective and protectionist exemptions in the bill are concerned. Going through these exemptions by the present government, it is apparent that the burden is put on the lower income group to pay for the government's wasteful spending. It has always been my view that the first criterion of a national legislation is universality. If this tax is to close the gap between compensation payments and export tax revenues, this should be another reason for the legislation to be universal, for everyone to pay. A selective measure like this one is always discriminatory, because it once again burdens the workers, who should be the first to be exempted if we are to have exemptions.
I read the bill a number of times to try and find out why the minister introduced such a legislation. What was his purpose? I found some kind of an answer in one of his statements, that the bill will help stimulate-and nothing less-the use of public transit. Such a statement is the end of it. Since I was first elected here we have been fighting for improved passenger transportation, and even now we are fighting to maintain what is left of the remnants of CNR services, and lo and behold! The government says it intends to reorganize and encourage public transportation. That is the best one I have heard so far in this session.
What improvements does the government propose? Will it finally convince CNR's technocrats to stress service before profitability? In those rarefied spheres, they strive for profitability but we say that in public transportation, service should be the first priority. So today, they are proving us right because they wish to promote service. Let them give adequate passenger services, good public transportation, and then let the 10 cent tax stimulate workers to use such public transportation, but there must be public transportation in the first place.
As things now stand the 10 cents per gallon tax is directly affecting workers. In large centres, with measures proposed by the minister to reorganize bus services or public transit, it is going to be easy or at least easier than in our rural areas. I feel sure that if they want to, the ministry can provide adequate service to people in large centres. According to his estimate, this policy will save a good deal of energy and in this manner travels will be restricted or, in cities, the use of private automobiles for workers driving to work will be restricted.
As far as cities are concerned, the idea may be of some value, but in the country it will not work as, at the moment, there is no public transportation system. The man who leaves his community to go to work in the next

town absolutely needs a car, which is his main working tool and now it is on this very tool that a tax is imposed while all others are exempted.
In the bill, as far as exemptions are concerned, those who could afford to pay are exempted. Here are a few examples, I quote:
(a)	Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province or any agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province,
(b)	a person for commercial or business purposes-
This means that all industrialists and businessmen will be able to get a rebate. Yet, there has also been mention of farmers and fishermen, which is quite acceptable. However, there is another matter to be resolved: How will the rebate be made?
Mr. Speaker, thousands of inspectors go around and search the houses of our farmers since this famous tax has been invented. This often gives heart attacks to the farmers. We shall have to distinguish between gasoline used for farming and gasoline used for pleasure. I do not know what regulations will be invented, but I know that it will take an army of inspectors to check on each farmer and to check each bill to determine if it was really used for the purpose indicated. The same will apply to businessmen and those who will benefit from thee rebate.
In my opinion, in addition to being unfair to the small wage earner, this bill discriminates even against the farmers and the fishermen. It will provide an excellent opportunity to create new protected jobs since these taxes, that will be just sufficient to pay all the inspectors and the inspections costs, will have to be collected. I am certain that the money collected will be just sufficient to pay all these people and to get all other small wage earners fed up. This is another measure that is aimed at providing jobs for people in the party. It is favouritism aimed at bleeding those who go for a drive with ten gallons of gas in their car instead of their truck or tractor without reporting it. If the inspector finds out, the farmer will pay a fine, and I imagine that the investigations will multiply. Mr. Speaker, we all know what can happen when there are investigations.
The bill will be passed and this is why we have to talk as though it already had been passed. I would like to ask the minister, who had to leave the House, or his representative-he can read Hansard-the Minister of National Revenue, who said the other day to the press, and I quote:
Not a gift. The Minister of Revenue pointed out, yesterday, that the reimbursement of the 10-cent excise tax on each gallon of gas to users of vehicles to business or commercial ends will be taxable-
Notice that: they take with one hand and grab with the other.
-will be taxable, contrary to what the Minister of Revenue, Mr. Ron Basford, indicated earlier in the week.
Indeed, on Monday, Mr. Basford stated that the tax announced in the June 23 federal budget would not be subject to tax.
It will be taxable. Imagine! After telling the farmers, "You will be exempt; give us your receipts and we will reimburse you the 10 cents a gallon." Right after, one hour later, they are told they will be taxed. What a joke! It is as a result of problems such as those that farmers, fishermen, those who are supposedly going to be exempted, are in fact
July 21, 1975

going to be fooled; once again, they will say: The act seemed to do all right by us, but again it will mean nothing. Once again, it is meaningless.
That is the only kind of bills we study in depth, and then pass here. The big shots are protected, those who could afford to pay the tax. That is why I say we would be better off levying a luxury tax on alcoholic beverages. Those who can afford to drink, let them be taxed: I could not care less. I don't mind alcohol or tobacco being taxed three times more than now. For my part, I do not smoke. That does not make any difference. That would be favourable to the health of our general population.
But they are taxing a sector essential to our family heads, to our workers, and we are going to accept that straight away, Mr. Speaker. It is impossible. A little further, the minister told us that the bill would contribute, they claim the purpose of this bill is to remedy the recession and fight inflation. Just another reason the minister gave us. That ghost of inflation behind which the minister hides is a myth which the population is now used to.
When he wants to be serious, the minister knows perfectly that any new tax causes an increase in the cost of living, thus kindling inflation. Let's stop considering our fellow citizens as stupid, because they suffer in silence all government extravagancies. I hope only one thing: that the awakening of the population be not so violent as to send our parliamentary institution over board, because of the lack of seriousness or, even worse, the lack of responsibility of the present government.
I will conclude by saying that all we can say will certainly not change anything to the situation, but at least people will know we have fought fearlessly against such action. We will vote for the amendment of the opposition, to postpone for six months the discussion of the bill, and we will vote against Bill C-66.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening with interest to the debate last Wednesday when the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) said there was nothing good in the budget. Having been caught once remarking that there was something good in one of the minister's budgets and being quoted thereafter, he said this time that there was absolutely nothing of any use in this budget. On that point I almost agree with him but, after a great deal of examination, I did find something useful in it.
On what page?

On page 28 of the budget speech when the minister said:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to announce that the government will be introducing legislation to increase the rate of return on existing Government of Canada annuities.
This is a piece of legislation to which we are looking forward, and I wish it were in front of us instead of the present bill. It would move a lot faster, believe me. That is the last kind word I have to say about the budget.

The minister does not say what percentage increase it will be.
Excise Tax Act

This is something about which the elderly citizens in my constituency are left in doubt. I do not see why the minister could not announce what the percentage increase of these annuities will be. I suggest that he could increase them 100 per cent and make a good case for it. I believe the payments are computed on a 4 per cent annual interest rate, but I think that 8 per cent would be a reasonable return in these days of expensive money and inflation, caused by this government. I would think that anything less than a 100 per cent increase in the annuity payments would not be satisfactory.
However, now that I have covered the good point in the budget I would like to make another brief comment about it. At first I thought it was a good point that the minister appeared to have spared us his usual sneaky little trick of dropping taxpayers from the tax roll. I have sat in the House through about three budgets and I have read several more which were brought down before I came here, going back to the Benson budgets when the Liberal minister of finance one year claimed to have dropped one million taxpayers off the tax rolls, and the next year
800.000.	One year 400,000 were dropped, and the next year
500.000.	Do you know, Mr. Speaker, that of those millions of people I have never met one?
At the start of the speech the minister would announce the raising of exemptions and he would say that they dropped off so many taxpayers, and then later in the speech he would announce the raising of the income tax. So these are a kind of recycled taxpayers. This time the minister has done it differently. He claims to have cut the budget by $1 billion. So this year he is recycling billions of dollars instead of taxpayers. I suppose that this might be considered an improvement.
At page 14 of the budget speech the minister stated:
The government has therefore decided upon a wide ranging set of measures, covering our statutory as well as our non-statutory programs, budgetary as well as non-budgetary spending, our salary as well as our hiring policies. All are directed to bringing outlays under more effective control and to slowing down their rate of growth this year and into the future. Our target of cuts this fiscal year is $1 billion.
That sounds great until you look a little farther along at the tables on page 40 where you see the title "Government of Canada Revenues and Expenditures on a National Accounts Basis". Under the year 1974-75, preliminary actual, total expenditures, you find $30,678,000,000. In the next column under the year 1975-76, forecast, you find $35,845,000,000. So the minister has stopped dropping people off the tax rolls and increasing the number somewhere else, and has chopped $1 billion from the budget. Miraculously it turns out to be a $5 billion increase.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but I wish to bring to his attention that we are not debating the budget at this time but rather Bill C-66, an act to amend the Excise Tax Act. The budget debate is over. I am prepared to give the hon. member all the latitude this House will allow, but I hope that he will soon come to his remarks about the Excise Tax Act modifications which are before the House at this time.

I read with interest several of the debates which have taken place in the last few days and.

Excise Tax Act
with respect, it seems that some hon. members managed to get quite a considerable distance away from this bill.
They were all Tory speeches.

I had hoped for an opportunity to reply, particularly to the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez), and to some of the charges he made about the government of the province of Ontario, which at the time did not seem to me to be particularly relevant to Bill C-66.
I would like to read from Hansard for July 16 where the hon. member for Nickel Belt said:
For the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton to castigate the Liberals for the kind of mean legislation they are introducing-is to forget, Mr. Speaker, that the province of Ontario takes 19 cents on every gallon of gasoline for the provincial coffers.
That being in order on July 16,1 would like to reply to it on July 21, if I might. Such a thesis is advanced by the hon. member for Nickel Belt. I can say quite sincerely that he fulfills all the requirements for a good socialist speaker in that he is able to speak quite irrationally on a subject, but with the utmost conviction. The thesis he advances would prohibit people from speaking about this tax bill if they were of the same political faith as the government in the province in which they live and if that province has a tax which is levied on gasoline.
On should perhaps think of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who is present tonight. I presume the hon. member for Nickel Belt is claiming that there is no gasoline tax in Manitoba and none in Saskatchewan, but I happen to know that there is in B.C., and I am informed that there is also a gasoline tax in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Yet I would be the last one to deny the right of the NDP to castigate this defective bill on the excuse that they should not be allowed to because their particular brand of government has a tax on gasoline in their province.
In British Columbia it is interesting that the gasoline tax was recently increased two cents per gallon. God knows most of us know enough about politics in Canada to sympathize with provincial governments because of the very narrow taxation fields left to them. There are few ways for them to raise funds for highways other than a gasoline tax. In B.C. the NDP government decided not to use the tax levied on the poor driver to repair highways or build new highways. Instead it is being put to a most peculiar purpose. In British Columbia for many years there was a pretty healthy automobile insurance business, which paid in taxes on premiums something in the order in 1970 of $2.9 million; in 1972, $3.2 million; and in 1973, $3.7 million to provincial coffers.
This made the NDP government rather envious, and its members thought the companies must be making enormous profits, so they thought they would take over that business, and of course with government expertise in all these things they thought they would do extremely well. They took it over, and the resulting loss in tax revenues to the provincial government by this monopolizing of an industry is $3 million to $4 million per annum. On top of that this government company has managed to lose $35 million. The industry was quite healthy when the government took it over, and to make up for the $35 million it managed to lose, the government imposed a gasoline tax

increase. The poor driver in B.C. has to pay for the inefficiency of the Socialist hordes, and it comes pretty hard at times.
I would like to make one small comment on the claim made by the NDP, not in this debate but on this subject, that the main fight which is going on in this House regarding the budgetary measures of the government, including this ten cents excise tax, is coming from the NDP. This was stated by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) on, I believe, the CTV network. Of course I can never hope to reach the audience the hon. member had in order to correct him, but he said that he thought that the main battle against this iniquitous budget was coming from the NDP. I would like to point out that a quick scanning of the pages of Hansard during the six days of the budget debate indicate that on June 25 there were four speakers, one of whom was a New Democrat.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext: It is quality that counts.
Where were the others?

That I do not know. On June 26 there was one New Democratic speaker of nine members who spoke: on June 27 there was one NDP speaker of nine members who spoke; on July 2 there was one NDP speaker of 13 members who spoke; on July 3 there was one NDP speaker of 13 members who spoke; and on July 4 there were no speakers from the NDP and 12 from other parties. This came to a total of five NDP speakers-out of a total of 60 speeches made-putting up the battle and the real opposition, according to the hon. member for New Westminster, to the budget. This is some fight, the greatest since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) started wrestling inflation to the ground, and it has had about as much result. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

Mr. Speaker, during the dinner recess I had an opportunity to look over the remarks I made earlier today concerning the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Leggatt) and his allegations about the NDP fight against the budget. It occurred to me that not all Hansard readers would identify him as the TV personality of the convention. It was the hon. member for New Westminster whom the commentators kept saying should have been running instead of the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent). I am inclined to agree with them.
However, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby is to be congratulated on his pre-ordained victory-ordained primarily in the offices of the giant multinational unions. It is one of the ironies of Canadian politics that the party with the word "democratic" as part of its name should
July 21, 1975

conduct such an undemocratic leadership convention where nearly half the delegates were not elected by their neighbours but instead were selected by the giant multinational unions. These organizations thought so little of the convention that they sent only enough delegates to guarantee the election of their choice.

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: Out of order.

The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby should be congratulated.
Looking at this budget bill, C-66-

speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board
speechtext: It's about time.

-I would like to remark that I am a great admirer of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and his department in the House during the last seven months. During question period we had the experience of the minister for five months saying that he could not answer questions because he was waiting for his budget measures to work their way through the economy. Then came a change and in April he could not answer any questions because he was bringing in a new budget. Maybe he is getting into a seven month cycle where we will have a new budget every seven months, followed by a period in which he will not answer questions on his budget measures, saying he must wait for them to have a salutary effect on the economy. Then there will be a period preceding the next budget which is meant to rectify the miserable failure of the previous one.
I should like to ask the minister if he had considered an exemption, in Bill C-66, for handicapped people from the ten cents per gallon excise tax?

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The minister is not here; his parliamentary secretary is not here.

Many handicapped people are absolutely unable to use public transportation. Some have gone to great expense to have their cars modified and some have built special ramps to enable them to wheel themselves into their cars. It seems to me unreasonable and cruel to charge these people this ten cents per gallon excise tax.
I wrote to the minister some time ago about this matter. After the usual cordial salutation he replied:
The department has received a number of representations asking that some deduction be allowed in respect of transportation expenses for the handicapped, particularly in respect of their expenses incurred getting to and from work. Therefore, the proposal has previously received considerable study. In general, deductions in computing income are allowed either in respect of amounts incurred to earn income or in recognition of a particular circumstance which necessitates the incurring of abnormal expenses. For tax purposes, disability is recognized as necessitating relief in two forms, namely, through medical expense deductions and in a special exemption for the disabled.
Unfortunately this only applies to people who are bedridden or in wheel chairs. A great number of deserving handicapped Canadians are unable to qualify, not being bedridden or in wheel chairs, so I think it is unfair of the minister to suggest that he is all heart when it comes to every bedridden patient who cannot work. He should also worry about those who with a great deal of effort are able
Excise Tax Act
to go to work. He should find it possible to do something for them. The letter continued:
Transportation expense is an expense highly dictated by personal choice and subject to a number of widely varying conditions.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, this is tommyrot when talking about disabled people who have no choice of transportation.
The letter continues:
Because of the broad difference in the amount spent for transportation and the range of circumstances which influence the amount spent, nearly all tax systems follow the rule that no general deduction is permitted for personal transportation expenses.
Dismaying as it was to receive such a reply to representations made on behalf of my constituents, I had hoped that the minister might find it possible, in his budget speech at least, where he made several other exemptions, to do something for these people. Such was not the case, however, despite the fact that Bill C-66 makes some exemptions.
On page 2 the bill gives the right to rebate as follows: 47.(1) Where gasoline has been purchased by
(a)	Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province or any agent of Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province,
(b)	a person for commercial or business purposes,
(c)	a farmer for farming purposes,
(d)	a fisherman, hunter or trapper for commercial fishing, hunting or trapping,
(e)	a person under conditions for which relief from the consumption or sales tax is provided by virtue of any provision of this act other than subsection 27(2), or
(f)	a person within a class of persons exempt from tax under part I of the Income Tax Act.
I think a considerable percentage of the population must be covered by these provisions so I find it strange that the minister could not make an exception for the few handicapped people who depend on transportation to get to work.
I checked on the number of people involved and, although it is difficult to get the figures, I learned that in the province of Ontario there are 3,867 people driving with licences limited to those cars which have an automatic gearshift or an abridged clutch-brake system. Presumably since there are 3,867 such licences in Ontario there are that many handicapped people driving cars. It would be fair to say, surely, that there are about 10,000 such people in Canada, every one of whom is required to drive a special type of car, at additional expense, and every one of whom is making a sincere effort to be part of the work force, despite the handicap. If each person uses, say, two gallons per working day, each person will use 400 gallons a year; at ten cents per gallon, times 10,000, the minister would collect an additional $400,000, or $40 per person.
I know that there is a legend in this House. Mr. C. D. Howe once said, "What's a million?" He said it in the days when $1 million was a lot of money. Surely as the budget contemplates the spending of about $35 billion, the minister could look favourably on the request of the handicapped, who want to deprive him of only $400,000 out of his income exceeding $30 billion. If the minister cannot

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
exclude these people, I ask him to consider giving them the right to rebate.
I note that the minister said on July 9, when participating in debate on the Excise Tax Act, as reported at page 7410 of Hansard:
Nor was it in the national interest that the excise tax on gasoline be paid by hospitals, or by educational, welfare, and charitable organizations.
I think he can stretch that a little and include the handicapped. Or, in the alternative, the handicapped ought to be allowed to band together as a charitable organization, and therefore come under the provisions relating to charitable organizations. But I point out that these people are independent minded. They do not wish to band themselves together and accept charity. They wish to be as self-sustained as possible and are willing to do everything they can to maintain themselves as independent members of our work force.
I look forward to this debate being carried on in the committee stage, in two or three weeks time or whenever it happens to be, when we shall all have the opportunity to speak as often as we want. I hope to ask the minister some definite questions concerning his intentions with regard to the handicapped. It saddens me to see that, after having received my representations by letter, he should introduce a measure like this which will so clearly hurt those people, and that so far he has refused to do anything to make their lot easier.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to express unequivocal support for my leader's amendment to Bill C-66, which would hoist this bill for six months. I find it strange to note that no government members are rising to speak. Not one has risen to speak since last week. Obviously they fear this bill, and run from the House. I suggest that there is complete chaos over on the government side with regard to implementation of this legislation. The implementation provisions were to be explained fully by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford). Is it not strange that he has not spoken on the bill? I hope these matters will be made clear before the debate ends.
There is very little in the latest budget that would lead anyone to believe that it will be of benefit to anyone in the nation, let alone the nation as a whole. The proposed excise tax on retail gasoline is probably the best example of the discrimination that is running rampant in the government's recent thinking. This measure will certainly produce some blatant discrimination against the groups of individuals who are already carrying the greatest tax burden on their shoulders at this time. I refer to the working people who produce the goods and services that keep our country going and prospering, despite the best efforts of the government. The latest mish-mash of tax increases has landed squarely in the laps of the same people; and these are the people who have no legal way to retrieve their tax dollars. They cannot afford to "buy" the loopholes that many affluent members of society can. And they do not have a huge margin of extra income to draw on when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) decides that they should carry an extra load.

I accept the concept of the two-price system for oil and the benefits of fuel for Canadians at less than the international price. But I cannot ask any working person in any part of this country to carry the load for me by way of an excise tax on gasoline. This is exactly what this budgetary measure calls for. I cannot understand why people living in Stonewall or Headingly, Manitoba, and happening to work 15 or 20 miles away, in Winnipeg, should have to pay an extra ten cents per gallon which they cannot recover, so that we can have a two-price system for oil. There has to a more realistic method to raise the funds required, a method that would have every taxpayer in the nation bear the burden equally, and not single out certain individuals who can least afford this burden.
There is a score of methods by which this job could have been carried out more effectively, and certainly more fairly. This makes one think it very strange that this budget was even produced unless it was simply the result of compromise amid a disagreeing cabinet. If this is the case then it is a splendid example of the old addage, "With compromise, everyone loses."
As has been stated before, we believe this matter could have been handled for the benefit of the Canadian people in a much more sensible and able manner than by the introducing of this very discriminatory tax.
Let us examine some of the alternatives. Foremost is some kind of a coherent transportation policy that will give individuals an alternative to the daily waste of gas they cannot avoid. Surely if the government had a genuine desire to conserve oil it would produce a transportation system which was a viable alternative to the automobile, a system which people would be enticed to use. Without doubt, if we had better passenger train operations in this country and some semblance of rapid transit systems in more cities, we could get more people involved in other modes of transportation.
Canadians are, in many cases, virtually forced to drive their automobiles to work. The result is a vast, unnecessary waste of gasoline. This, coupled with the higher costs occasioned by the new tax, means that working Canadians will have to ask their employers for more money. The individual employer will have to raise his prices to cover his own increased costs, and the circle continues, with a higher inflation rate as the inevitable result.
This proposal for taxing gasoline at ten cents a gallon will result in about $525 million in revenue. The oil subsidy program is estimated to cost about $400 million. Even if one did agree with the government's archaic methods one would have to note that the revenue is excessive by over $100 million. This is over kill.
It will be argued that the full ten cents, while unnecessary, will result in greater conservation of energy. I submit that the effect on conservation will be negligible. The people I mentioned, those who must drive to work, cannot choose not to buy gasoline. Until public transportation systems improve the present situation is a fact of life. For people who can afford to drive for pleasure, ten cents a gallon makes little difference. The effect of the conservation measure of these people will be nil.
Until the government can show an example of restraint and conservation in its own back yard, any of its words on
July 21, 1975

this subject will be treated as the total hogwash they are- and that mild word is being used only out of respect for parliament, for which we still have feeling on this side.
If the government had any real commitment to saving, there are hundreds of things it could do. This has been said before, but it will keep on being said until someone on that side begins to listen. The government could cut out some whole programs. Certainly some LIP and OFY projects are questionable. If the Liberals could do without their publicly funded propaganda arm, easily half the budget of Information Canada could be cut. They could and indeed must cut back on the billion dollars a year that is spent on outside consulting services.
If the government were serious it would exercise a little more common sense before introducing an unnecessary expenditure the size of Petro-Can, a move that had to be the greatest example of inappropriateness until this budget was introduced. It was totally inappropriate to introduce a tax measure that is going to raise inflation by 2 per cent during a time of unprecedented high inflation. It was totally inappropriate to introduce a measure that is supposed to force people to conserve gasoline by using public transport when public transportation is non-existent for 80 per cent of the working people in the country. Also, it was totally inappropriate to introduce a tax that is blatantly discriminatory against the working poor and the working people at a time when these groups are already being taxed to death by all levels of government.
The government has the unmitigated gall to call for conservation when its own shameful, irresponsible waste is the very reason for the bulk of the country's woes. I find that the very lowest form of hypocrisy.
A great deal more can be said about the implementation and administration of this tax. It was the botched up result of the short sighted thinking that we have come to expect from a government that has apparently lost sight of reality of the practical considerations and consequences of its actions.
The tax was levied against the refiners and importers of gasoline, and the date of commencement was set at June 24, 1975. The gasoline in the hands of wholesalers and retailers on which the special excise tax had not been levied should have been available to consumers at the pre-tax price. However, this was often not the case and the retail price immediately jumped at many pumps. A little more thought by the government to alternatives, such as a date of commencement on July 1, might have helped to avoid the problem and a fair number of consumer rip-offs.
Some other major problems with this excise tax have to do with the administration of the refund claims and the very question of who will be exempt. The question has been raised about municipalities not being specifically referred to in the bill. I wonder what other groups have been inadvertently left out of the exempt categories. This was very fully covered this evening by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). Notwithstanding this, the volume of paper work involved in processing the exemption claims will be staggering, probably resulting in a further expansion of the federal bureaucracy to handle it.

This runs contrary to the supposed purpose of the budget, to restrict the growth of the public service.
It is pretty obvious that this bill has been very poorly drafted and will result in an administrative nightmare. I can only hope that the government will see fit to swallow whatever pride it has salvaged and co-operate with us in attempting to improve the situation and the legislation.
I have outlined the reasons why I feel this legislation is inappropriate, unrealistic, useless and damaging. It is obvious that it is dangerously inflationary at a precarious time for our economy.
Worst of all, it is doing expressly what the Minister of Finance has vowed not to do, that is, fight the country's economic battles on the backs of the working poor. With the ineffective strategies being employed in this war there will be an awful lot of broken backs before it is all over.
In a recent newsletter the Canadian Chamber of Commerce summed it up very well. They are certainly in tune with the Conservative party in their thinking about this bill. I quote from the newsletter:
"Unless there is an immediate end to the battle between governments for resources industry revenues," said Mr. B. T. Johnson, Chairman of Executive Council of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, "the real loser will continue to be the consumer. The ability of the industry to find and develop new sources of supply is hampered by the lack of money."
"The Canadian consumer should not be misled into believing that the recent increases in petroleum prices are providing large profits to the petroleum industry," said Mr. Johnson in a statement released today. "In fact, by taking larger and larger tax bites without regard to their impact, the federal and provincial governments have become the real beneficiaries of recent price increases."
"The latest $1.50 per barrel increase authorized by the federal budget of June 23 is a classic example," he said. "Unless the producing provinces reduce their royalty rates the entire $1.50 will continue to be taken by the federal and provincial governments until December 31, 1975, and thereafter the governments will receive approximately $1.25 or 83 per cent, while the industry will retain about 25 cents or 17 per cent and then only provided there is a very substantial re-investment of funds by the industry in exploration and development. This is equivalent to a wage-earner receiving a $1 per hour increase in wages and taking home only 17 cents."
Mr. Johnson said, "The Chamber is concerned that the actions of some provincial governments have further reduced the revenue that should have been available to the industry, by the temporary freezing of prices and/or the requirement of applying to a provincial board for approval to implement the federally-authorized price increase."
"Such interference in the competitive market system," said Mr. Johnson, "artificially reduces prices for a short period with little benefit to the consumer, causing the industry to lose millions of dollars that would otherwise be available to develop new sources of supply and assist Canada to regain its self-sufficiency in petroleum products in the 1980's."
"The consumer should also know where the money goes when he buys a gallon of gas at the service station," said Mr. Johnson. "Off the top of the retail price in Montreal of 78.9 cents per gallon, the federal and provincial governments take 32.3 cents including the 10 cent-per-gallon excise tax imposed by the recent federal government budget. The service station operator receives about 10 cents per gallon. Of the 36 cents per gallon balance, approximately 12 cents is paid out in royalties and income taxes. A similar breakdown applies across Canada, varying only with the application of provincial taxes and retail margins, leaving 24 cents to pay for exploration, drilling, extracting, storage, refining, transportation, marketing, wages, interest on borrowings and other costs."
In summary, Bill C-66 is highly inflationary. It is in direct conflict with the government's so-called consensus plan which was announced some weeks ago. The consen-

Excise Tax Act
sus plan was to deal with inflation. However, after a few meetings with business and labour we heard no more. The plan apparently died, and inflation continues to run unchecked in Canada. When will the minister and the government bring in proper legislation to deal with inflation?
Has this government no compassion or conscience? I beg them to stop the double-talk and window-dressing consensus plans and act now before they completely destroy this country.
It is the Progressive Conservative party, the official opposition, which has led the fight to,oppose Bill C-66. As the Liberal member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson), who is the Liberal member for Winnipeg South, will be voting for this huge tax increase, I will be the voice for these two consituencies and vote against this bill on their behalf as well as on behalf of the residents of Winnipeg South Centre.

Mr. Speaker, I will try not to cover too much old ground that has been sort of mulled about in the chamber, although I cannot help but comment on a couple of features that other speakers dealt with at some length.
I think it is important that we talk about the bill instead of a number of fairly unrelated matters. This bill is clearly a regressive piece of legislation, the kind one can expect from a Liberal government, a government that is very cautious at election time about the great Canadian population. But between elections we have grown to accept this kind of cynicism, this kind of bill which clearly has the same kind of impact on someone earning $30,000 as on someone who is earning $7,000. Its effects will be least among the elite, among certain people in the business community who can deduct this iniquitous tax; but my constituents, who have to drive to work every day, really do not have any choice. We cannot expect people who have to drive 20 miles every morning through the Fraser Valley into Vancouver to stop driving simply because they feel the tax is too high. We cannot expect them to stop consuming gasoline.
I wish to deal with the spurious argument that somehow this tax contributes to the conservation of gasoline. The hon. member for Rocky Mountain (Mr. Clark) dealt at some length with the problems of those who occupy themselves with the affairs of their community in a practical way, people who have a socialist regard for the common good and who volunteer their time as necessary.
That spirit was there long before socialism.

They are now being told it will cost them more to make their contributions to the community. I would not expect to see this kind of legislation around election day, so I suppose we have a long way to go before we see another federal election.
This tax bears heaviest upon those who can least afford it. It will cause approximately a 2 per cent increase in the cost of gasoline. The man who motors 15,000 miles a year

will pay an extra $75 to $90 for his gasoline. Oil for home heating, as a result of the minister's proposal, will cost an extra $60 a year, again a regressive tax.
The principle of the equalization of gasoline prices in the country is one which commands general support, but the manner of achieving it boggles the mind when one thinks of the options available to the government. If they wanted to end the fixed write-off for corporations they could pick up another $500 million. If they wanted to end the investment tax credit they could get another $200 million. That would quickly provide the kind of revenues they are looking for.
It would cost a few jobs, I suppose, particularly in some areas.
It might cost the Liberals a few supporters, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Don't get nasty!

I suppose we have to weep most about the oil companies. These people I see every Saturday night tell me it costs a lot of money to drill in the Beaufort Sea, and that it is necessary to make big profits if they are to drill in this country. And the government has gone along with this point of view.
Poor old Imperial Oil! In 1971 its profit was $136 million; in 1972 it was $151 million; in 1973, $228 million, and in 1974, $290 million. We are facing a strike in this country and it is the oil companies which are on strike. They won't look for any more oil because $290 million is not enough. They need more! And they know where to look for more.
Take poor Gulf Oil. In 1971 it made a profit of $53 million; in 1972 profits rose to $64 million, and in 1973 the figure was $101 million. That little oil company is growing. It is doing very well. But not well enough to go out and explore for oil. They have to look after the shareholders before they do that.
The government has been put into a panic by the protests of the oil companies that their profits are so low they cannot afford to look for oil. I shall not pursue this aspect of the matter; I believe the topics I have dealt with so far have been pretty well covered by my hon. friends and others.
On July 9 the minister stated, as reported in Hansard at page 7409, that this tax would contribute significantly to energy conservation, an objective which the people of Canada support. I question that statement, Mr. Speaker. I am sure the hon. gentleman is right when he said this was an objective Canadians support, but to say that raising the price of gasoline by ten cents is likely to lead to the conservation of gasoline is meaningless. As long as the automobile ethic is with us, people will continue to use gasoline. No one has challenged that ethic. No one has come forward with a concept capable of leading North American society away from the automobile.
The minister mentioned conservation three times in the course of his speech but nowhere did he tell us how we could promote conservation, save for this suggestion that if the price were high enough it would deter purchasers. In fact the record in the last ten years shows the opposite to be the case. The price of gasoline has been climbing steadi-
July 21, 1975

ly even in the absence of this last ten cents impost. On the other hand, consumption has been increasing at an even faster rate. The record gives the lie to the minister's argument that raising the price of gasoline would deter people from using it. Let us cease making spurious arguments and direct ourselves seriously to the issue of conservation.
The other gesture the minister made toward the conservation of energy was to remove the 5 per cent sales tax from insulation materials. This is a meaningless gesture, for the simple reason that the retailers themselves do not control the price of the product. The companies which produce this material control the price, so the tax relief will be gobbled up by the major companies which control production.

I want to assure Your Honour, with the greatest respect, that I am not intending to violate the rules of the House by speaking from the wrong location, but it is easier for me to stand in the aisle.
If I can return to my train of thought, it is alleged that the removal of the 5 per cent sales tax is contributing to the conservation of home heating oil, but this is meaningless since most heating oil is consumed within the home. What we should have had is a complete reduction from income tax of the cost of insulating one's home, perhaps with some provision being made regarding the building of a home. Gestures like this are not encouraging the Canadian people to go along with meaningful conservation.
British Columbia has had a 55 mile an hour speed limit for I do not know how long, but this is unknown in the east. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) made certain suggestions regarding conservation in 1973, but in our house we were taking those steps
Excise Tax Act
five years before that. We are waiting for the rest of the country to catch up with us.
I suggest we should do something about the horsepower rating of cars that are imported into Canada. Some cars gulp gas at the rate of one gallon for every nine miles, some even every five miles. Surely the government has the courage to take a forward step in that regard. I notice my good friend from Oshawa-Whitby indicating skepticism at that remark, but again I think this would be a useful step to take.
We could also stop building these monolithic skyscrapers in the centre of our cities which make enormous demands on our energy resources, and redirect some of our priorities in more meaningful ways. We could do something even more important, and that is to implement a Liberal promise made in the last election regarding rapid transit. However, it looks as though my hon. friends on the other side are following a well known maxim, which is never to spoil a good promise by keeping it. The promise to provide rapid transit was a good one, and let me put it on the record, as reported in the Montreal Gazette. On June 17, 1974, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in Toronto announced a $270 million program to aid public transit. He said:
A Liberal government would pay 100 per cent of the cost of Canadian-made commuter vehicles and 50 per cent of the cost of platforms and stations. The government would also pay 25 per cent of the cost of Canadian-manufactured vehicles for public transit within cities. Encouragement and assistance would be given to smaller municipalities in the creation of new transit systems, Canadian industry would be encouraged to develop passenger vehicles, and experimentation with new transit systems would be assisted by federal financing of demonstration projects.
That would be a good start, and it is something that the Canadian people endorsed by the way they voted last time. I respect the way they voted. We took a shellacking in the last election, and we are perfectly ready to admit it. They wanted to take another chance on my hon. friends opposite because they wanted that kind of leadership, a meaningful approach to conservation and changing the lifestyle of this country with regard to the automobile. But what action does the government take? It puts a ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline. Is this the government's response to the over-consumption of energy in this country? I suggest it is a meaningless gesture.
One of the problems in this country is that consumption of energy is determined by those who advertise to a great extent. I am tired of looking at advertisements placed by hydro-electric companies urging people to buy a toaster or a refrigerator, and then on the next page there is a news report which says the same company requires another dam because it is short of power. We cannot have it both ways. Much of the energy demand in this country results from consumerism on the part of companies, and the oil companies continue to be among the worst offenders. We are letting demand determine supply, which is something we cannot do if we want to change our lifestyle.
This demand is artificially created and maintained to some extent by the oil companies, the electric companies, by people whose interest it is to see that over-consumption of energy continues. The government does not have the courage to interfere; it is still sitting there, living with Adam Smith. What the government must do is to enter the

In March, 1975, the Science Council of Canada made a statement of which the government has not taken notice but which I recommend be read very carefully. In its report No. 23 it said this:
Traditionally Canada has allowed projections of energy demands to dictate policies for energy supplies; little thought has been given to the efficiency with which we use our energy resources.
What the Science Council is trying to say is that we should change our demand concept or we will not make any progress at all with energy conservation in Canada.
I suppose one of the tragic things about the whole question of conservation is that Canadians are squandering energy and we still have not got together in a conservation effort partly because of lack of leadership by the government. We are the second highest energy users in the world. We spend eight cents of every dollar on energy, or 18 cents of every dollar on energy using facilities. This waste in the eye of anyone from an energy poor country would be seen as a national scandal. How to we change this situation? We do not do it by playing a game with an excise bill and calling it a conservation bill.
This is purely a revenue producing measure. It is not a popular bill. It would never be introduced at a time when the government would have to stand or fall on its legislation. This brings us back to whether the government has the courage to do some unpopular things. I am not one who would always stand up and condemn a government for doing something that is not entirely popular. I do not think that would be a quality of leadership. The government should show once in a while that it can do that, rather than bring in such an excise tax bill.
The government should have a meaningful program, one in which perhaps there would be the necessity to take a look at rationing. It should be a program for the conservation of energy, in which high users would be charged less. At the present time high electricity consumers are given a reduced rate while the smaller consumers are charged the full rate. Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like to say I was concerned a little by the effect the proposals made by the minister in this budget would have on the constituency I represent, as well as on the country as a whole.
As the minister went through the list of proposed expenditure slashes it became evident that there were areas which would definitely effect my constituency. He spoke of defence, the environment, trade and commerce, the farm Credit Corporation, and the Business Development Bank. I was forced to question some of his priorities.
Two days ago when we had the announcement of the scrapping of the urban demonstration project I received a phone call from the reporter of a local radio station who asked whether I did not consider, with hindsight, that the budget had been one that struck particularly hard at the constituency. I reminded him that it did not require any hindsight, and that I had told him exactly that on budget night in my remarks following the presentation of the budget.
We are debating an amendment which would hoist the bill and I believe this is in line with the thinking of a great many Canadians who, at the present time, are wondering why the minister bothered to bring in a budget at this time. We wonder at the thinking which allowed him to be trapped into presenting a budget at a time when it was neither wise nor necessary to do so.
I think the budget that was presented is indeed a strange one. The main purpose of it would seem to be to assist inflation because we find it lacks the courage to hit the issue of inflation. It demonstrates a lack of courage to bring in any effective income policy. The minister has presented proposals which in a time of inflation are inflationary. He brings in a ten cents a gallon tax on gasoline on top of the increase in the price of oil. This is a particular blow to a constituency and a province which depend on the tourist industry, because here we have a proposal guaranteed to reduce travel within the country and to discourage entry into the country by those who would drive across the border and contribute to our revenues in the west, or in any other part of Canada for that matter.
I should like to return to the question of the collapse of the urban demonstration program because it has been touted as one of the great savings in the budget. We are led to understand that close to $100 million is to be saved. That program originally was announced by the present Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford). At that time the present minister did not hold the portfolio. I have here the brochure that was prepared when the Minister of National Revenue was the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. At that time the program was announced with great fanfare and some very fine words. In the preface to the brochure we find these words:
The Canadian Urban Demonstration Program is one way of helping to ensure that as change comes, as it must, it will be in the direction we want. The program is designed to identify and highlight the best of the new ideas Canadians have for improving their communities. By encouraging and publicizing successful innovations across the country, a more genuine choice will be open to everyone who will affect our
July 21, 1975

urban future: elected representatives, officials, private interests and individual citizens.
It ends with these brave words:
I wholeheartedly encourage your participation in this exciting new program, through which Canadians can play an active role in the shaping of their future.
The history of the urban demonstration program is such that it certainly will not encourage Canadians, be they elected officials, representatives, or private citizens, to become terribly excited about any future program brought forward by the federal government with this sort of fanfare. Anyone who sees what has happened in respect of this program would be very discouraged about the prospect for the future.
I should also like to quote from the section of this brochure on financing the program, where we see this:
It is expected that the basic cost of demonstration projects will be financed through normal sources of funds: federal, provincial, municipal, private, or any combination of these. Additional support may be provided from a $100 million fund that will be disbursed over five years, beginning April 1, 1975. The fund is intended to be a catalyst and supplement, not a source of prime capital financing.
We know now that the operative words there are the "may be" words.
In spite of the reference to the $100 million fund, Canadians and particularly municipal officials who were lured into applying for money from this fund, found out that no such fund ever existed and that the savings are paper savings-that the financing was not there. There were 14 projects accepted initially. Then the minister sought to cancel the entire urban demonstration project in spite of the size, quality, and great words of the brochure.
The public might have been led to believe that there was a direct connection between the bringing down of the budget and the ending of the program. In fact there might be some Canadians who assume that that was the entire cause of the end of the program. But we know from various press reports that other factors were involved.
The first 14 projects selected for the program were screened by a now defunct advisory committee headed by Dr. Kenneth Hare of the University of Toronto, a former federal adviser on environmental research. In a statement reported in the Ottawa Journal of Monday, July 7, Allan O'Brien, the advisory committee member, is quoted at some length. The article says that the program's suspension did not particularly surprise him. He said he was disappointed because the program did have potential to develop and expand the federal government's role in government affairs, and he criticized the implementation process designed for the program, saying it had not been thought through carefully enough. That, of course, is not the first bit of government business in recent years that has been announced prior to its being thought through carefully. He repeated that the advisory committee had been in limbo for some weeks while federal officials tried to figure out what its function should be in the future.
So when we learn that the entire program has been scrapped we can be a little skeptical on this side of the House in assuming it was scrapped because of anything that came out of the budget. I think the program was in a
Excise Tax Act
mess and that the decision, which had been hailed as being a very tough one on the part of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), was perhaps not all that tough.
When we look at the highlights of the budget, on page 5 of that handy little brochure issued along with the budget, we find the section on the control of government expenditures, reductions and postponements, indicating they will be applied to almost all government departments and agencies, and some of these are singled out for special mention. They are Transport, Defence, Public Works, Environment, External Affairs, Industry, Trade and Commerce, Secretary of State and other departments, Petro-Canada, the Federal Business Development Bank, the federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation, the Farm Credit Corporation, and others, but there is no mention of Urban Affairs, and no mention of the urban demonstration program. It seems to me very strange that if at the time it was prepared the people preparing it knew that the entire urban demonstration program was going to be slashed, there was not even a hint in the list of priorities for reducing federal expenditures.
The minister, in announcing the ending of the urban demonstration program, called it a suspension, but I think we can safely assume that it has been ended and will not be resurrected, at least until it serves the government's purposes to resurrect it. I suggest that the time for its resurrection will come during the next federal election campaign-which will undoubtedly be twice as expansionary as the one we had a year ago when all kinds of programs were being announced week by week as we approached July 8. Until then I believe the urban demonstration program is dead.
The total figure of the amount being saved is illusory because some 200 projects have been returned to the people who submitted them. I suggest that the municipalities and organizations which submitted these projects have made considerable expenditures in researching and preparing the applications to the federal government, and I find it utterly reprehensible that a government, which less than a year ago announced a project and urged, demanded, encouraged and incited municipalities across the country to apply for it, when it received the applications, withdrew the project.
An enormous waste is taking place in this country simply because senior levels of government have not seen fit to work out a formula whereby municipalities would share in the total tax cut in relation to the expenditures that are demanded of them. These expenditures are made mandatory by the senior levels of government, and yet the municipalities have to cover the total cost.
I feel very strongly about this, and I believe that in future before the federal government prepares a program of this nature and of this magnitude, and announces a fund of $100 million to finance it, whether it be over one year or over five years, it should have some sort of insurance program or be bonded so that the municipalities which apply in good faith, and submit applications meeting all the criteria of the program, could expect their applications to be taken seriously and be given the attention they deserve.
