There is a great waste when the federal government makes a sudden decision through which the entire effort that has gone into preparing applications is wasted and the program is scrapped. In many cases these projects are absolutely vital if we are to find a way toward solving some of the problems that beset the municipalities of this country. The federal government must give leadership and direction, which in this case it has abandoned completely and in haste to the detriment of the municipalities in Canada.
As we look through the bill we find one or two other areas which deserve comment. With regard to the tax on gasoline the government has left itself open to demands for refunds. As one reads the bill one finds considerable attention paid to individuals or corporations using gasoline on a business basis. I suspect it would be too much to expect of the government an extension of the system whereby agricultural gasoline would be coloured purple and farmers could use gasoline of the same grade in their machinery, thus avoiding the whole complicated business of rebates. One has to give the government some credit for its concern that this money be rebated, but one questions the whole proposal.
I notice nothing in the cancellation of the urban demonstration program to suggest that anything would be rebated to municipalities which submitted the 200 proposals. There is no mention of a rebate to mayors, aldermen, city engineers, and planners for the time they put into preparing those proposals that were scrapped so abruptly. I would suggest to the federal government that municipalities are made up of people, and people serve as mayors and aldermen of municipalities. They deserve better treatment than they have had from the government in the budget.
One suspects that we will have a very complicated few years as people submit their applications for rebates. Hon. members know the amount of mail we will receive from people who will be asking what happened to their rebates. They will wonder why they did not deserve a rebate, and we will find ourselves, as the ombudsmen of the people, sorting our way through unlimited numbers of applications for investigation of the whole question of the rebate. I can think of nothing which is more guaranteed to clog the mail, to waste time, to add expense and to save very little, in what is supposed to be a proposal to save gasoline and to push people toward rapid transit. I would suggest that although there has been a move to the cities and a great urbanization of this land, the government and the Minister of Finance should think very carefully before applying blanket taxes clear across the country which can be of no use in areas of the country which are decades away from any kind of rapid transit whatsoever.
It is doubtful whether this measure will accomplish anything in the urban centres in terms of increasing the development of rapid transit. It is strange indeed that as the ten cents per gallon tax is claimed to be for that very purpose, the urban demonstration project, which in many of its proposals was designed to hasten the development of alternate means of transit in the cities, should have been abandoned at the same time as the tax was imposed. Therefore, if ever there was an example of one arm of government destroying the efforts of another arm, it was

in the decision to abandon the urban demonstration program at the same time as the Minister of Finance imposed his ten cents tax on the people of this country.
One notices too that it is required of businessmen dealing with the gasoline to, and I quote:
-keep records and books of account in English or French at his place of business in Canada in such form and containing such information as will enable the amount of taxes or other sums that should have been paid or collected, the amount of stamps that should have been affixed or cancelled, or the amount, if any, that should have been paid or that is payable to him, to be determined.
There is no mention of compensating businessmen for that extra effort on behalf of the federal government. I do not know how many hon. members have been reading the mandate forms for May which have come in from small businessmen across this country, but it has been repeated over and over again, in comments which have been written in on them, that the federal government expects a small businessman not only to pay the taxes but to collect the money, and to do the endless hours of bookwork, without recompense or adequate compensation from the federal government. We will now have one more example of this, and there is a great revolt building in this country among those people who are opposed to being called upon to do the bookwork for the federal government. They are called upon to put in time, and occasionally to hire other people who are necessary because of the decision of the federal government to do this in an awkward and complex way which forces the businessman at the bottom level to keep records and books for the federal government. That is not good enough.
Finally, I would like to refer to one more part of the bill wherein the minister provides, and I quote:
Thermal insulation materials designed exclusively for insulation of buildings; storm doors and storm windows for buildings; articles and materials for use exclusively in the manufacture or production thereof
Will be exempt from the excise tax which remains from what had been an 11 per cent tax on building materials. On budget night I was not listening to the minister very carefully at this particular point, and I honestly believed that he had said that the 5 per cent tax was being removed from building materials. That is a move we on this side of the House have long advocated, and which is so eminently sensible that I could not believe any other course of action was being proposed. I went on the air back home in a telephone interview and said that the 5 per cent tax had been removed and that at last we had seen the end of that, only to learn to my surprise and horror that it was nothing of the kind.
Goodness knows I should be beyond the stage of expecting anything so sensible, straightforward, simple, so welcome to the lumber industry of British Columbia and so essential to the economy of the constituency I represent, which relies heavily on the lumber industry, as a complete removal of the last shreds of the unhappy and inflationary tax on building materials which has frustrated the economy and the businesses of this country for so long. I should have known that it could not and would not be done by the administration opposite, but I suppose it is the eternal optimism in my nature which leads me to believe that the government would actually do something very sensible.
July 21, 1975

When I heard 5 per cent and building materials in the same sentence on budget night, I leapt to the conclusion which I hoped the minister would have been worthy of but of which he was not. Instead, we have this tiny little removal which goes along with the window dressing which bedecks the entire budget, a suggestion that basically the government is endeavouring to save our fuel resources when it has not begun to tackle that; a suggestion that it is fighting inflation when it has not begun to tackle that.
The budget failed completely to tackle the problems which beset this country, and because in the Excise Tax Act it fails to do anything sensible it has aroused the people of this country as few measures this government has undertaken for many years have done.
I support the amendment which would hoist this bill for six months, and I hope forever.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have been following the debate on Bill C-66, to amend the Excise Tax Act, with a great deal of interest. Much has been said about the lack of equity in this bill, and while I do not want to repeat many of the arguments I think it would be useful to summarize some of the effects of this bill.
Usually one can see bad effects of a particular piece of legislation, and generally it is easy to see that some segment of society will benefit. In the case of Bill C-66 it is easy to see that the bad effects will be felt by many. The bad effects will be felt by workers who are forced to drive to work because of shift work, because of a lack of public transit, or because they live in the suburbs.
Cities will suffer because there will be increased pressure to locate one's residence close to the work location and close to existing public transit systems. Businesses will also suffer, particularly the small businessman who may be a marginal operator. This small business category also includes farmers, fishermen, travelling salesmen, and neighbourhood servicemen. Although the small businessman will get relief in the form of a rebate of his tax, he will have to bear the additional costs of carrying the amount on his books from the time the tax is paid at the gas pump until his refund comes, months later.
Furthermore, the small businessman will have to bear the added cost of accounting for the tax, completing an additional complex government tax form every time he has to apply for the rebate, and of calculating the additional income tax payable on the rebate after it is received and included in income. I will have more to say about the income tax effects of the bill later.
Also feeling the adverse effects will be senior citizens, the physically handicapped, and people who cannot take advantage of public transit for a variety of reasons.
It may be asked who will benefit from this bill. Will it be big business? I say no. They will incur extra costs in financing the huge extra amounts they must pay at the pumps. They will incur extra staff costs for filing claims and generally overseeing this taxation exercise.
Excise Tax Act
It is interesting to note that the government suddenly woke up to the fact that business would be getting an advantage under the original proposal, so now the rebate will be required to be included in income for tax purposes.
Will the oil companies benefit? No. The president of a major oil company said recently:
No matter what sort of face the government tries to put on it, the important thing for the public to realize is that none of the funds resulting from the new ten cent per gallon excise tax on gasoline or the $1.50 per barrel crude oil price increase will go to the oil companies which need the money for exploration.
Will the public generally see any benefit from this bill? No again. As usual the public will be paying and the government will be spending. The government's proposal to spend exploration dollars through its new Crown corporation, Petro-Canada, was of course the subject of long debate in this House recently.
Who will benefit then? It is no surprise that it will be the government and the bureaucrats. The government has gained a huge new source of revenue at the expense of the individual working Canadian. The bureaucrats have gained a huge new bureaucracy to collect and administer the tax, much of which will be refunded under the expemption provisions.
I think it may be interesting to note what the minister said in his budget speech in June. He said:
Gasoline purchasers from the commercial, industrial, resource and government sectors will be able to recover the tax. For example, refunds will be available on gasoline used for commercial trucking, for service vehicles, taxis and buses. Similarly, the tax will be refunded on gasoline used in farm vehicles and fishermen's boats. The tax on gasoline used for construction or industrial purposes, or in oil and gas, mining or forestry industries, will be refundable. Gasoline purchased by governments, including municipal, are also outside the scope of the tax.
Imagine what proportion of gasoline in this country is used by those exempted-the taxi industry, the trucking industry, buses, service vehicles, farm vehicles, the construction industry, general industry, the extractive industries, and governments at all levels. I would guess that the proportion would be as high as 80 per cent, but the government has given us no indication of the percentage of use it expects to be exempted from the tax.
The government claims that the ten cents tax is in part a conservation measure. As with the equity arguments, there seems to be no unanimity on that. In a recent speech in Ottawa the Liberal member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) said:
As a conservation device, the new excise tax is unrealistic and is also unfair to millions of Canadians. It implies a government view that for essential family purposes like food shopping and visits to physicians, can turn to alternative forms of public transit instead.
In the same speech he said later:
The only practical way for millions of Canadians to travel to and from work is by car. They either have no adequate rapid transit-or no rapid transit at all-available to them. None will exist for many years in most urban areas. And in some areas, the remote parts of the country and smaller cities and towns, none will likely ever be constructed.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, not all of the opposition is on this side of the House.
Earlier in this debate the hon. member for Skeena (Mrs. Campagnolo) said that the tax is an unpopular one and that this legislation is not popular legislation. Many mem-

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
bers on the government side are silent on this issue and their electors will wonder why.
I was interested to see a letter in the Globe and Mail this morning from a Liberal member of parliament who shall mercifully go unnamed at this moment. He received many letters from constituents complaining about gasoline prices-"not so much about the ten cents tax" he wrote, although that tax was clearly part of the complaints. He had written to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) in part as follows:
What is so irritating to the people of this region is not the current price level or even the ten cents per gallon excise tax but rather the huge differential in prices.
This Liberal M.P. requested that an inquiry be initiated to determine the reasons for these wide variations. Perhaps he thinks the federal government should just set the price of gasoline at the pump instead of just applying the unpopular ten cents tax.
You should read it all.

I read it all this morning, but I think the important part is adequately covered right now.
Not only are constituents unhappy with this bill, action such as this in Bill C-66 does not promote good will with the provinces. Ontario, for example, has moved to implement a temporary freeze on gasoline prices, and other provinces may follow. Fearing a slump in the demand for automobiles produced in North America and the lay-offs that would result, Ontario removed its 5 per cent sales tax on North American produced automobiles for the rest of 1975.
The federal government seems to have ignored regional differences in other ways too. The amounts being denied the producing provinces by the imposition of a lower than market price on fuel does not help the residents of nonproducing provinces because they are being called upon to pay a price per gallon nearly the same as it would be if the world price were paid for crude oil. The difference is that the extra money paid is going to the government coffers and not being used to explore for more oil supplies or to encourage more enterprise in the petroleum industry. Nor is it benefiting the provinces that have the constitutional right to the energy.
I should like to look at the detailed workings of the government proposals now. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in answer to some opposition criticism in the House, has asked the question, "How would you do it?"
If we were to accept that the government needed a huge increase in its tax revenues, it seems to me that the Minister of Finance already had the tools at his disposal to carry out his program without resorting to this ten cents per gallon "refundable-if-you're-lucky" tax. But if its interest was in the conservation of resources, the senior government could have used its persuasive powers to reduce speed limits on a nation-wide basis. Slower speed is a proven saver of gasoline and lives, as shown by the experience in the United States.
The federal government has not been hesitant in passing laws about automobile safety and emission controls. It certainly has the power to take other conservation measures such as limiting engine size or even requiring the
[Mr. Clarke (Vancouver Quadra).}
installation of mechanical "governors" on automobiles to limit speed.
Before suggesting further government action such as the foregoing I would point out that the government's inappropriate and ineffective attempts at conservation would be unnecessary except for the fact that the government has enormously reduced the capability of the petroleum industry by its interference with such measures as the disallowance of provincial royalties as a legitimate business expense in arriving at taxable income; the artificial setting of wellhead prices below world market levels; the setting up of a national petroleum corporation; and the passing of tax rules favouring foreign investment in petroleum exploration.
Before anyone jumps up to say that I favour Canadians paying higher prices for gasoline, let me remind the House that the government's proposals will have exactly the same impact on taxpayers as would a world market wellhead price. The money all comes from the Canadian taxpayer. If the government pretends otherwise, it is deluding you.
The past few remarks refer only to conservation aspects. The Minister of Finance seems to have forgotten that the government has a rather large collection agency known as the Income Tax Department, which has grown enormously in order to deal with the Trudeau government's principles of simplicity and equity in regular income tax matters. Nobody in authority has any idea what happened to the simplicity or equity. The task of this department will be expanded to include the collecting and refunding of the ten cents per gallon tax. Imagine the addition to the bureaucracy that will be required to handle the processing of all the claims. Don't forget that every exemption will result in a monthly rebate to be processed.
On the other hand, if the government would admit that the sole or main purpose of the tax is to produce revenue, and I am not advocating a tax increase when I say this, just think how simple it would have been to raise this amount of tax revenue by increasing the rate of income tax by a point or a fraction of a point.
Let us look at the result of such a move, and who would be hurt or helped. First, Canadians on very low incomes, including many retired people who are among the hardest hit, would not incur any cost at all since their incomes fall below the taxable level. Second, Canadians not entitled to any rebate, including industrial and office workers, and physically handicapped people, would pay a little more income tax instead of a little more in excise tax, and the net result there would be about the same. And the load would be shared more equitably since the amount would be determined by income level instead of by the number of miles driven to work or to the grocery store. Third, the effect on businesses would be about the same as for wage earners if the government decided to increase income taxes instead of taxing gasoline. That is, business would pay a larger and fairer share of the national revenue. Businessmen, after all, are taxpayers, too, and if Canada needs more revenue they should be required to pay their share.
July 21, 1975

Under the budget proposals contained in this bill the ten cents per gallon tax is a complete washout for corporations and for businessmen, no matter what their marginal rate of tax is. Because the ten cents per gallon paid at the pump is deductible in computing taxable income, the net cost to the businessmen at a 50 per cent marginal rate is an extra five cents. When the ten cents rebate is finally received it must be included as taxable income, and five cents income tax must be paid, leaving a net refund of five cents. Therefore, we can see a net five cents outlay and a net five cents rebate, bringing a washout effect. But of course the corporate bureaucracy will have grown in order to deal with the filing of claims for rebates and the general recording of and accounting for these additional and completely unnecessary transactions. This increase in corporate staff will, or course, be mirrored by the huge increases in the government bureaucracy which will handle its side of the collections, the administration, and rebates. Truly, the taxpayer will be the loser on all fronts.
My remarks today, Mr. Speaker, have been specifically directed to clauses 5, 6, 7 and 8 of Bill C-66. This is not meant to indicate any agreement on my part with clauses 2 and 3 which will increase the air transportation tax from 5 per cent to 8 per cent on flights to the United States, and will double the air transportation tax to $10 on flights to other countries. I might only point out that this can hardly be construed as an anti-inflationary move by a concerned government. And, as with the oil industry, the airline companies, already hard pressed by rising costs, will not receive any of the increases in the fares created by this tax.
Clause 4 is perhaps a small concession to the taxpayer. We find that, while dipping into the taxpayer's pocket for taxes on gasoline and air transport, the government will make it easier for the taxpayer to drown his sorrows. It will reduce the excise tax on wines by 20 cents or 40 cents per gallon, depending on alcohol content. Perhaps the only good thing about this bill may be that, under clause 4, the stronger the wine is and the more you drink of it, the more taxes you will save.
All the provisions of this bill give credence to the good intentions of the minister and the benevolent Liberal government. Their fault is in the execution of their aims, not in their desire to be big brother to all Canadians.
In order to convince Canadians what good fellows they are, the government has been trying to fool us into believing that the Liberals are a united party, the only truly national party in Canada. But now the official report on the 1974 election results, released last week by the Chief Electoral Officer, shows that the Liberal party led the pools in only four of Canada's 12 provinces and territories, whereas the Progressive Conservative party led in seven of those 12 jurisdictions. Furthermore, whereas the Progressive Conservatives came second in five jurisdictions, compared to the Liberal party's six second places, the government was embarrassed to finish third in one province and one territory. Furthermore, the Liberals can boast of holding the reins in only three of Canada's ten provinces. Without question these statistics show that the Progressive Conservative party is the only national party in Canada.
Excise Tax Act

Mr. Speaker, the budget was introduced almost a month ago, and the budget has made necessary the introduction of this excise tax bill.
Last June 23 I personally experienced two apparently unrelated events here in Ottawa. For the first time in my life I paid 20 cents to use a pay telephone. Second, I saw the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) introduce a summer budget. These two events are very much related, of course, since both show Canada's extreme situation relating to inflation, the cost of living, and costs of production.
A month after budget day, the real blockbuster of that budget comes in Bill C-66, which of course is the new ten cents a gallon excise tax on gasoline used for personal consumption. I shall talk mainly about that aspect.
In my opinion, this tax is intended to be a straight revenue producer for the government. It remains to be seen how efficient it will be in view of the complex and expensive administration and refunding procedure which will need to be established. It will generate some $350 million in the remainder of the present fiscal year and thereafter will generate over half a billion dollars annually. This figure implies that some five and a quarter billion gallons of gasoline sold in Canada will be taxable under this new provision. Based on 1974 gasoline sales of seven and a third billion gallons, this means more than 70 per cent of gasoline consumed in Canada will be taxable in the personal or pleasure category.
Those entitled to a refund are estimated to be between 750,000 and one million people, but owing to multiple claims for refunds that are expected this year, this could total $170 million. That is approximately $1 refunded for every $3 collected. Surely it is a most inefficient and expensive tax to collect.
The government has already endorsed a single price system for petroleum products on a geographic area basis, whereas this bill establishes a two price system based on consumption. Therefore this will most certainly create additional burdens on certain sectors of the Canadian economy.
As we are now in the middle of our tourist season, this is where the first impact will be. In fact it is already being noticed. Already there are clear indications that Canadians who had planned a truly Canadian vacation by car have had to shorten their trip or re-route them to the United States where there is cheaper gasoline, cheaper lodging, and cheaper food. This is Canada's loss, of course, in more than just the monetary sense. It follows that this ten cents tax will definitely curtail our United States tourist friends from spending their vacations in Canada.
We in western Canada will feel the impact of this tax relatively more because of two main factors; less public transit, and longer distances that are travelled on the prairies, mostly by farmers. These longer distance costs should be allowed for in this bill, but they probably will not be. They will be included in the "personal use" category.
I want to give a personal example. From my home on my cattle ranch it is a 20 mile trip just to get my mail. There

July 21, 1975
Excise Tax Act
are no rural deliveries. It is a 100 mile trip to do business in either Medicine Hat or Maple Creek, such as for groceries, haying supplies, or some emergency welding. There was a time when some of these trips were made with horses, but that is very seldom done now. My point is that under prairie conditions cars are a necessity, not a luxury. This tax could very well perpetuate regional inequities in our more sparsely populated areas.
Whether the tax will result in some energy conservation remains to be seen. I am inclined to agree with the Canadian Automobile Association when they suggest, and I quote:
Imposing excessive taxation under the guise of energy conservation and forcing motorists to utilize public transportation is unacceptable. With 85 per cent of all passenger trips in all Canada undertaken by automobiles, and the majority of Canadians requiring their car for transportation to work, it is impractical to force Canadians into public transportation by economic sanctions.
I would add, especially on the wide open spaces out west.
There will be some reduced consumption of fuel, I am sure. After all, a ten cents per gallon increase is a record tax bite. It will get some results. However, if we are realistic we must realize that Canada cannot conserve enough to ensure adequate supplies for the future. That can only come from a vigorously stimulated exploration and development policy. The new budget will probably increase some exploration. However, one estimate of a $40 million release to the industry is only enough to drill one offshore well in the high Arctic.
The budget speech points out that Canadian oil export tax revenues have fallen off while oil import subsidies have risen, hence the need for this gasoline excise tax. The two are obviously related, but not to the extent suggested by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) in his letter which appeared in last Saturday's Ottawa Journal. The letter is headlined "Oil firm's ads were misleading." The minister stated, and I quote:
The ad, headlined "Here's where your money goes for those gasoline price increases", refers first to the 10-cent excise tax on a gallon of gasoline announced in the June 23 budget and proclaims: "100 per cent to the federal government."
That is 100 per cent wrong. Not a penny of that 10 cents will go to the federal government. The purpose of the tax is to keep home heating costs down by permitting the continuance of the oil import compensation program. The revenue-all the revenue-from this tax will pass to consumers in Eastern Ontario, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces in the form of reduced prices for petroleum products, including home heating oil.
I am sorry the minister is not here tonight. I would be tempted to say to him "Come now, Mr. Minister, by the same token I suppose not a penny of my income tax goes to the federal government. It is just some sort of a miracle transfer to pay my share of federal welfare, unemployment insurance costs, pensions, and so on." I suggest a fair percentage of that ten cents will be required to pay the administration costs of this tax, and the government is collecting every cent of it. Who is misleading whom?
In summing up my comments on this ten cents excise tax portion of this bill I want to say it is the abruptness and the magnitude of the tax that stagger and hurt so many Canadians. As crude oil prices move up it is inevitable that gasoline prices must also move up some, but could not the tax have been staged a little more humanely,

such as over at least two years? This ten cents blockbuster could very well stampede car buyers away from the bigger models to the compacts and the mini-compacts, and in so doing create undue problems in the auto industry.
If I may, I want to comment very briefly on some other aspects of the bill.
I should like to associate myself with many others in this debate who have commended the Minister of Finance on removing the 5 per cent tax on building insulation materials. At the same time I ask the very logical question: why not from all building materials? There never was a better opportunity to do something to improve the serious housing situation.
In addition I will mention one very specific and relatively small budget item-removing last year's excise tax on domestic wine. It is strange indeed that the minister should have zeroed in on this one item, both in the budget and in the bill before us, and that no mention at all should be made about the serious tariff and quota problems at the U.S. border involving the Canadian cattle industry.
I have a final comment relating to another very specific budget item-it may not be referred to in the bill before us, but I will mention it only briefly. The rate of return on government annuities is to be increased. This is very good news, of course, but it is news which is long overdue. Could the minister or, in his absence, the parliamentary secretary, announce very soon what the new rate will be? Will there be a COLA clause? Will this change be retroactive? I am getting letters concerning these three questions.
In conclusion I wish to say I fully support my leader's amendment to this bill giving it the hoist to you-know-where. I would urge hon. members on both sides of the House to go home to their ridings during the summer recess, whenever it comes, and learn the real grass roots impact of this measure by talking to their constituents about what Bill C-66 will do. I am referring mainly to the ten cents a gallon excise tax.

speakeroldname: Mr. A. D. Alkenbrack (Frontenac-Lennox and Addington):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider it a privilege to enter this debate and speak in support of the amendment put forward by my leader some days ago to this bill, Bill C-66, which constitutes an assembly of financial arrangements resulting from the budget. The measures we are asked to approve will be of no benefit to the Canadian economy or to the Canadian people and their future welfare.
I think the budget, and Bill C-66 which emanates from it, are best described by an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on June 24, the day after the budget was brought down. That paper describes it as a "tinkering budget". The heading reads: "The budget tinkers again". The writer describes it as a failure of leadership in a situation which has rapidly deteriorated. And it has deteriorated since then. Canadian affairs are in a state of decline. Indeed, I would not be at all surprised to see this country faced with a financial crisis before the snow flies in December. I hope this does not happen, but the general condition of our economy as reflected in the various departments and the various services the government is attempting to carry on presents a picture in which I can
July 21, 1975

see nothing but deficits and a very poor outlook. This is why I would not be surprised to see a financial crisis before the fall.
The Globe and Mail continues on a sad note:
-if the upturn ever does come, Canada, with first year new contract wage settlements averaging 19.2 per cent will simply not be in a position to compete.
This places us in a very sad situation. I continue to quote from this leading article:
The Finance Minister says he faced three dilemmas in shaping this budget-inflation, unemployment, energy. About inflation he does virtually nothing. His promise of federal spending cuts of $1 billion this fiscal year must be as suspect as all his other figures. He does not even promise to freeze the growth of an overgrown civil service; only to reduce its rate of growth.
I shall quote no further from this editorial except for the final sentence, which reads as follows:
What this budget says is that Canada is in deep trouble and virtually leaderless.
To my mind this is a sad situation for us to be in after the Canadian people have given the government such a generous mandate. I refer again to the phrase I quoted from the Globe and Mail-that Canada should be virtually leaderless.
We have the spectacle before us of a government which imposes a ten cents a gallon surtax on gasoline and in the same stroke of the pen removes the tax from wine. What could be more ridiculous? That is one for the books. May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MINISTER'S ESTIMATE OF RATE OF GROWTH THIS YEAR
speechtext:
I am sure the minister does have an unavoidable engagement but it would have been quite easy to
Adjournment Debate
ask that the debate which is to take place tonight be held over until another occasion when the minister could appear. I say this because I have stated three times in a row that the minister had misled the House. The situation to which I shall refer hon. members is one in which the minister, after being prodded twice, admitted he misled the House. I believe hon. members are entitled to have the minister appear and explain why he has misled them in the way he has.
The Minister of Finance is no longer credible. He has chosen to bring in budgets and make statements in the House without giving members the benefit of the forecasts upon which he is basing his statements and budgets. Let me refer to a question that I put to the minister in the House on July 18, as reported at page 7655 of Hansard:
As the minister has repeatedly stated that he has always been frank with the Canadian people, and in view of the anticipated high inflation rates, would the minister be frank enough to tell the House and the people what he anticipates will be the real rate of growth in Canada in the current year, a figure he gave in each of his four budgets for each year but not in his June 23 effort?
The minister replied:
If the hon. gentleman would read the budget speech carefully he would find that I estimated the rate of growth at somewhere between zero and one per cent.
At three o'clock that day I rose on a point of order to point out that no place in the budget of June 23 is such a statement made by the Minister of Finance, to which he replied that he would send me the reference. Again the following day I rose on a point of order to point out that I had not received the reference to which the minister referred, and suggested that perhaps under pressure the minister had mistaken his answer with a statement he made to the first ministers' conference, at which time he commented on the poor growth in the gross national product in the current year. At my second prodding the minister then admitted, as reported at page 7711 of Hansard for July 18:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is perfectly correct. Those numbers were given in the speech I made at the federal-provincial conference which was tabled in the House by my parliamentary secretary, and the budget reflected those figures.
The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the minister is wrong again. The figure that he gave on Thursday of last week of zero to one per cent real growth in the economy for 1975 was not the figure that he used at the federal-provincial conference to which he has now referred. Perhaps we can understand why it is that the minister has chosen to fail to give us an inflation rate for the country, and has failed to give us the unemployment rate anticipated by his department, and has now failed to give us the real growth rate, when we check the record of his previous forecasts. In short, we find that the minister has muffed every forecast that he has never given in a budget concerning real growth in Canada.
If hon. members review the May 8, 1972, budget they will find that the minister predicted in the 1972 year under review that the growth would be 6 to 6l/2 per cent; the actual growth was 5.8 per cent. In the February, 1973, budget which predicted that the real growth would be in the order of 7 per cent, it turned out to be 6.8 per cent. On

July 21, 1975
Adjournment Debate
May 6, 1974, he stated that the real rate of growth would be 5 per cent higher in 1974 than 1973; the real growth was 2.8 per cent. In the November 18 budget, on which many members of the House spoke, the Minister of Finance predicted growth this year would be 4 per cent; we now find after the tabling of the budget on June 23 that the minister did not even have the courage to tell us on what real growth figures that budget was based.
The minister did not have the courage to tell us the figures because he knows that the figures are growing worse and worse month by month. According to the recent forcast of the Conference Board of Canada the gross national product in real terms is expected to decline by approximately .6 per cent in 1975 over 1974.
Imagine, Mr. Speaker, here we have a Minister of Finance assuring us on November 18 that the real growth in the economy of Canada in 1975 would be 4 per cent; he does not have the courage to tell us what it is going to be today; yet we find the Conference Board of Canada predicting a negative growth of .6 per cent. Having misled the House on two former occasions the minister has not had the courage to come to the House and explain why he so misled the members of the House.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-MINISTER'S ESTIMATE OF RATE OF GROWTH THIS YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one is reminded of the saying that none are so blind as those who will not see. Here we have an example of the phrase, much ado about nothing. The minister conceded in the House that when he referred to the fact that the comments he made were contained in the budget speech they were contained in the papers that were tabled by me on his behalf in respect of the federal-provincial conference. There was no suggestion of hiding anything.
The question concerns the prospective real rate of growth in Canada in 1975. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) said in this House on July 17 that he estimated the rate of growth at somewhere between zero and one per cent. The main forces in play were set out in the budget, but it may be helpful to the House for me to recall them and bring them up to date. When all the data is in, the rate of output in Canada in the first half of 1975 will almost certainly be recorded as smaller than it was on the average in the last half of 1974. But real growth in output is expected to resume in the second half of this year.
Much of the most important factor in the slowdown in real output in Canada has been the rather large and sharp recession abroad, particularly that in the United States. But now, with every passing day, the prospect of economic recovery in the United States and Japan in the second half of the year appears more likely, along with at least a cessation of the decline in output in western Europe. These are powerful forces working toward increase in the real level of Canada's exports in the second half of 1975.
The indicators of consumer confidence in Canada did not fall to anything like the low levels they reached in the United States in the last year; and they are now strengthening. Automobile sales held up remarkably well in Canada compared with the United States during the last nine months. There is every prospect that real demand for consumer goods and services will grow moderately over the next six months. In most recent months one of the

depressing factors on production in Canada has been the correction of what had developed as an excess inventory position. The correction needed in Canada has been much smaller than in the United States, and the process of correction is well advanced. Accordingly, before the end of this calendar year at least moderate inventory rebuilding should be under way. Crop reports are reasonably good to date, though there are some worries about sufficient moisture to produce good harvests.
All these factors add up to a realistic prospect of positive real growth in Canada in the second half of the year, barring very severe work stoppages, and bad weather. With this second half growth to offset the real decline in the first half, we expect the year as a whole to show a rate of growth over 1974 of the order of one half of one per cent.
I do not think it was necessary for the minister to be here to make that statement again for the edification of the hon. member.

MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH AND STUDENT SUMMER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMS-REQUEST FOR EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 18 I directed a question to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) relating to the fact that the unemployment rate for those citizens of Canada in the age bracket between 14 and 25 had reached serious proportions, particularly among students who were trying to find funds to increase their education.
I asked the minister whether he would take action in the immediate future to expand the programs which were already in existence under the student summer employment program for 1975. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, I appear here tonight in view of the fact that I cannot accept the answer given by the minister wherein he indicated that his government had considerably increased the allocation to the student summer employment program. Even though I must accept his answer to a certain extent, I cannot accept the statement that the government is doing everything possible to deal with the problem, particularly with the means available under the student summer employment program.
I want to refer to only two phases of the 22 programs designed to provide opportunities to Canadian youth. I refer to the cadet training program and the militia or reserve training under the Department of National Defence. Under these two programs some $700,000 will be allocated to cadet training, and $4.2 million to the reserve forces or militia training. I might say that the Government of Canada is prepared to allocate funds amounting to some $5 million, but it is ignorant of the fact that many thousands of our young people are denied the opportunity of taking advantage of the cadet and militia movement under the aegis of the Department of National Defence.
I might say, as an experienced advocate of the Department of National Defence, that I am sorry to see that the
July 21, 1975

Government of Canada in directing the Department of National Defence is not taking advantage of its capability of providing leadership, esprit de corps and comradeship even though the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) and the chief of our armed forces keep repeating year by year that the Department of National Defence will build up the armed forces of our nation in peacetime through the militia and the cadet services. But over the years nothing has been done, only lip service has been paid to the goal. Even though the government has the capability of providing leadership and instilling esprit de corps and comradeship in our youth, I can only say that more consideration should be given to providing greater initiative with the aim of building a better future for Canada. I ask the parliamentary secretary to reply to my question.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: MANPOWER-OPPORTUNITIES FOR YOUTH AND STUDENT SUMMER EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMS-REQUEST FOR EXPANSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like many other hon. members, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall) has been a strong advocate of the role that students could play in the summer program of the Department of National Defence. At the same time I have to say that he threw me a slight curve because his question tonight was initially directed to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) and I think it is more appropriate that I respond on behalf of that minister. Perhaps he can put another question on another "late show" to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson).
The hon. member will recall that the question of growing youth unemployment and the possibility of increasing funds available to the OFY program in order to combat the problem was dealt with in the House on February 24, 1975. At that time the minister pointed out that a total of $67.1 million had been set aside for the federal government's Student Summer Employment and Activities Program (SSEAP), of which $27.5 million had been allotted to OFY, the largest recipient program.
The allocation to the OFY program, as with the allocation to the other components of SSEAP, was set after applying statistics of past demand and trends to the estimated youth employment situation. After a review of the allocation to the 1975 program in light of increases in the rate of student unemployment, an additional $13.4 million was allotted to SSEAP in an effort to compensate for such increases. Of these additional funds, $8.9 million was used to augment the OFY budget, allowing for the creation of 7,000 extra jobs under that program. With this considerable increase in funds, more than 250,000 student jobs have been created either directly or indirectly within the framework of SSEAP, a total of 27,000 of them within the OFY program.
With the instigation of such measures to deal with the problem of student unemployment, the minister is satisfied that the problem has been significantly alleviated, and no expansion of OFY or SSEAP is foreseen at the present time.
With respect to the comments of the hon. member directed to the Minister of National Defence, perhaps we can get together again some night, and I will have a good answer for the hon. member on that one as well.

EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ATTEMPT TO EXPEL ISRAEL FROM UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) what Canada's answer would be to the 50 states, members of the United Nations, who intend to seek to expel Israel from the General Assembly this fall. I wanted a clear statement from him of unwavering support for Israel, whatever the pressures. The minister has given Israel that support. He went on to tie his answer to the policy declaration of the government respecting admission of the Palestine Liberation Organization to Canada this fall to the scheduled UN crime conference which Canada is to host in Toronto. Wisely the conference is to be postponed until Canada is satisfied that a technical conference of the sort which this is intended to be will not be used as a weapon in the war to eliminate Israel.
The minister also committed himself and the government to contribute what he can by reducing tensions in the Middle East. The minister has taken the right course. I was surprised that the Conservative spokesman, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner), would try to minimize the role Canada can play in this matter. In effect he was belittling and downgrading the position of our country and the position we can take in resolving the tension in the Middle East. We of course are not the United States, we are Canada, but we are respected in the Middle East by all parties, and for our support in the past for the easing of tensions we deserve to be heard by the parties in the Middle East. As like all Canadians I look forward to an increasingly active role by the minister in that area of the world, and I hope the Conservatives will support him as will Canadians generally.
As one who called for the cancellation of the conference in Toronto this September I must say that I prefer the solution which the government has taken, a postponement until the UN atmosphere, in Canada's opinion, has improved. The government has not washed its hands of the UN or of the conference, in spite of the extent to which international politics and anti-Israel feeling have polluted it. Canada has drawn attention of the member states to a fact of which all Canadians are aware: to be effective, to be useful to its members, and to be worth preserving, the UN must return to its charter principles. These principles are respect for the integrity of member states, rejection of violence as a means of solving international differences, and universality of participation.

speakeroldname: Mr. Herb Breau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-GOVERNMENT POSITION ON ATTEMPT TO EXPEL ISRAEL FROM UNITED NATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as mentioned in the House of Commons today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), the position of Canada obviously is in favour of the principle of universality, and it will resist very vigorously any effort to change the status of Israel at the General Assembly.
The Next General Assembly of the United Nations will provide an opportunity to affirm the principle of universality as a fulfillment of what ought to be a basic aim of the United Nations. More specifically, we will resist any attempt to exclude Israel, or any other country, from the proceedings of the General Assembly. Acceptance of this principle would guarantee the status of Israel within the

July 21, 1975
Adjournment Debate
community of nations and thus remove one cause of instability in the area.
Through new initiatives, both bilateral and multilateral, the government will try to improve the political situation in the Middle East and in the UN, notably through our participation in the next session of the General Assembly, which may be crucial for the future of the organization, given the fundamental character of the issues on which debates are expected to focus. Canada will consult with other interested countries on the ground rules governing technical discussions in UN arenas. Either independently or in co-operation with others, we will attempt to formulate and seek support for an effective resolution in the General Assembly on this question.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs also intends to accept during the autumn outstanding invitations to
visit a number of countries in the Middle East. These visits, which the government already considered most useful for strengthening our relations with this region of the world, have taken a new urgency following the difficulties we encountered in holding the United Nations Congress on Crime Prevention. The House can be assured that the minister will take this opportunity to solicit the views of his hosts on these difficulties and seek their support for the United Nations as a universal forum and an effective international instrument.
